In a **[scathing takedown](https://arstechnica.com/space/2025/02/europe-has-the-worst-imaginable-idea-to-counter-spacexs-launch-dominance/)** of the [recent merger talks](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-02-03/airbus-hires-goldman-for-european-space-tie-up-to-rival-musk) between three of Europe’s space giants, Eric Berger’s ‘worst imaginable idea’ branding got one thing right: **Europe doesn’t have a SpaceX. But the merger isn’t about building one, either.**

Thanks for reading NebuLink’s The Business of Space! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Since the talks became public, critics have framed this as a “European Master Plan”, a bureaucratic attempt to create a government-backed rival to SpaceX. That narrative might drive clicks, but it is misleading. **This is not an EU-orchestrated industrial strategy. Airbus, not Brussels, initiated these talks, driven by market realities rather than state intervention.**

Unlike IRIS², the EU-funded broadband constellation aimed at reducing reliance on Starlink, this merger is not about building a SpaceX alternative. It is about consolidation in an industry that has long been fragmented by national interests and overlapping partnerships.

So why are critics so quick to dismiss it? And why do the comparisons to SpaceX miss the point?

## The ULA Comparison Is Flawed

In almost every single argument against the merger, **three letters keep coming up. ULA.**

For the uninformed, ULA stands for United Launch Alliance, an infamous joint venture between Lockheed and Boeing’s space launch operations that was forced upon the two companies by the US government after corruption scandals, the burst of the dot.com bubble, and legal battles between the two companies that threatened the future of the US domestic launch capabilities. A [brief reading of the background](https://spacenews.com/op-ed-ula-failure-of-merger-and-monopoly/) shows that both companies had completely different philosophies on how to deliver the exact same services. Lockheed selected a ‘dirt cheap’ Russian engine for their Atlas program whereas Boeing’s Delta had the first large liquid-hydrogen/liquid-oxygen rocket engine developed in the US since the space shuttle. The companies appear to have polar opposite business strategies, ideas, etc.

Imagine Lockheed Martin and Boeing as two stubborn roommates, constantly arguing about who gets to use the TV remote and who left the dishes unwashed. Fed up, the US government handcuffed them together and made them co-manage the household. Instead of cleaning and organising, they spent their time arguing over methods and who is right.

It shouldn’t come as a surprise that the ULA merger is widely regarded as a failure and is often used as a warning against mergers. However, not all mergers share ULA’s fate. When market forces drive consolidation, space industry mergers can unlock innovation and sometimes even success.

Maxar, one of the world’s leading space technology companies, has a long history of strategic mergers that have shaped its position in the industry. Over the years, it has combined expertise in satellite imagery, robotics, and space infrastructure through acquisitions and consolidations. These mergers have enabled Maxar to expand its capabilities in Earth Observation and satellite communications, demonstrating how well-executed industry consolidation can enhance competitiveness and technological advancement.

In general, a merger’s success relies on a shared vision for the future, strong leadership, and most of all, whether it is willingly entered into. Without this foundation, even the most promising synergies can fall apart. However, with clearly defined goals and streamlined integration, mergers can foster growth.

ULA’s failure was a case of forced consolidation without a shared vision. But not all mergers are doomed to stagnation.

# Airbus Has Done This Before

Unlike ULA, Airbus was not forced into an arranged marriage. It has spent decades using consolidation as a tool for growth rather than survival.

Airbus Defence and Space did not become Europe’s leading space company overnight. Its dominance is the result of decades of mergers and acquisitions, carefully integrating expertise from France, Germany, the UK, and Spain.

[

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/f610066e-c795-42fa-a348-d7b7c7800070_883x328.png)



](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qf_V!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff610066e-c795-42fa-a348-d7b7c7800070_883x328.png)

Figure 1: A simplified view of how decades of aerospace mergers led to the formation of Airbus Defence and Space.

If this merger seems like a radical reshaping of Europe’s aerospace sector, it is not. Airbus, Thales, and Leonardo already work together on major projects, often in overlapping roles. Rather than smashing together three independent competitors, this move formalises what is already happening behind the scenes.

The companies have already been working together on high-profile programmes such as IRIS², the EU’s secure broadband constellation, and Galileo, the region’s answer to GPS. If anything, the merger is a belated recognition that these companies already rely on each other to keep Europe’s space infrastructure running.

Take Thales Alenia Space, where Thales owns 67 percent and Leonardo 33 percent. It is already one of Europe’s top satellite manufacturers, producing telecom, Earth observation, and navigation systems. Then there is Telespazio, another Thales-Leonardo joint venture focused on satellite services, secure communications, and ground infrastructure. Airbus already works closely with both, so the merger is not about creating monopolies.

This isn’t a shotgun wedding… it’s just making official what’s already happening.

## Europe’s Airbus is No SpaceX… and That’s the Point

One of the more popular critiques of this merger is that it is Europe’s latest attempt to create its own version of SpaceX, a vertically integrated, fast-moving launch provider that can rival the United States. But that argument misunderstands both the nature of Airbus and the structure of Europe’s space industry.

SpaceX is a privately held company that integrates launch, satellite production, and broadband services under one roof. It thrives on rapid iteration, aggressive cost-cutting, and high-risk development cycles. Airbus, by contrast, is publicly traded, partially state-owned, and deeply embedded in European regulatory frameworks. Its business model is built on long-term contracts for defence, telecommunications, and scientific missions, not disruptive innovation.

This is not an attempt to build a European Starship or Starlink. The merger is about reducing redundancies, cutting procurement costs, and securing industrial scale for major European programs. Airbus has never been a serious competitor in the launch market, and its involvement in Arianespace remains secondary to its primary business of building high-reliability satellite platforms and defence technology.

## What this merger can and cannot solve

Bringing together three of Europe’s largest aerospace firms will have significant effects, but not in the ways critics assume.

This merger is about efficiency. Airbus, Thales, and Leonardo already collaborate on major European projects, but overlapping responsibilities slow development. Consolidation could streamline operations, free up resources, and improve Europe’s competitiveness in the global space market. IRIS², Galileo, and Copernicus all require extensive collaboration between multiple companies, slowing development. A single, consolidated structure could reduce the bureaucratic inefficiencies that have plagued these programs for years.

[

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/c24192ae-7ba1-4e93-9c8c-faad9c9587e7_641x176.png)



](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2HVu!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc24192ae-7ba1-4e93-9c8c-faad9c9587e7_641x176.png)

Figure 2: Half of the IRIS² industrial base is already composed of Airbus, Thales, and Leonardo entities, highlighting their existing collaboration in Europe’s space sector.

Stronger industrial coordination could also improve Europe’s global competitiveness. Airbus already builds secure military communications satellites for NATO and ESA, but European aerospace firms lack the scale of their American and Chinese counterparts. A more unified industrial base could change that, particularly in defence-related space projects where European firms struggle to match the sheer spending power of the United States, which allocated over $26 billion to space programs in 2023 alone.

But the merger will not fix deeper structural problems. European space policy remains fragmented, bogged down by competing national interests and slow-moving institutions. Merging Airbus, Thales, and Leonardo will not suddenly make ESA move faster. It will not fix Europe’s launch delays, nor will it create the conditions for a thriving commercial space sector. The merger does not change that reality.

If it collapsed tomorrow, it would not unlock venture capital for European space startups. It would not fix ESA’s painfully slow contract process, nor would it make European investors any less risk-averse. It does not force governments to rethink their reluctance to embrace a SpaceX-style model of rapid, venture-backed innovation.

The suggestion that Europe must decide between backing established industry leaders or fostering a dynamic NewSpace sector is a false choice. The reality is that Europe has already made its choice: it has spent decades propping up legacy aerospace firms while stifling commercial innovation.

At best, this consolidation makes an inefficient system slightly more efficient. At worst, it reinforces the same bureaucratic inertia that has held European aerospace back for decades.

## Europe’s Real Space Bottleneck: Bureaucracy, not Mergers

The real bottleneck is not mergers, it is a system that prioritises political interests over industrial competitiveness, making it nearly impossible for companies to scale, iterate, and compete globally.

ESA has become a funding machine for legacy aerospace firms rather than a driver of innovation. Its procurement system, shaped by rigid geographic return rules, prioritises national quotas over efficiency, carving up contracts across member states instead of selecting the best providers. This approach has led to cost overruns, inefficiencies, and delays. A [report](https://commission.europa.eu/topics/eu-competitiveness/draghi-report_en) led by former ECB president Mario Draghi flagged geo-return as a [major barrier to Europe’s space competitiveness](https://europeanspaceflight.com/eu-report-advocates-for-scrapping-esa-geo-return-policy/#:~:text=In%20a%20report%20commissioned%20by,competitive%20in%20the%20global%20market.), arguing that it stifles innovation and limits agility in a rapidly evolving industry. In response to mounting criticism, ESA has begun exploring reforms, but its entrenched procurement model remains a structural challenge.

EUSPA, the European Union’s Agency for the Space Programme, has only added more bureaucracy. Created to centralise European space policy, it has instead become an administrative extension of the European Commission. Every major initiative it oversees, from Galileo to IRIS², is bogged down by excessive political oversight and slow-moving decision-making. It lacks the independent, market-driven approach that has allowed U.S. commercial space companies to thrive.

Unlike NASA, which has channelled billions billion into private-sector innovation through programs like COTS and Commercial Crew, Europe remains locked into a funding model that prioritises control over outcomes rather than fostering competition. Instead of leveraging private investment, it keeps the industry reliant on state-driven programmes, preventing the emergence of a truly competitive commercial space sector.

## So, What Is Europe’s Answer to SpaceX?

If the Airbus merger is not Europe’s answer to SpaceX, then what is? The truth is, Europe is not even trying to build an equivalent. Its focus remains on institutional projects, not commercial disruption.

For years, Europe’s space policy has prioritised stability over disruption, institutional contracts over commercial competition. Nowhere is this dysfunction clearer than in the development of Ariane 6, a programme that embodies Europe’s struggle to balance political interests with industrial efficiency.

The result was a compromise that satisfied neither goal. **The problem is not the Airbus merger. The problem is a system that kills competition before it even starts.**

The real competition is coming from European startups developing reusable rockets, satellite constellations, and in-orbit servicing. There is **no European SpaceX** because there is **no European Commercial Crew** or COTS programme. There is **no pipeline for disruptive innovation because the system was never designed to support one**. Governments treat space as an industrial policy tool rather than an industry, ensuring that political deals dictate progress rather than technological advancement.

Without structural reform, Europe will not just fall behind. It will make itself irrelevant. The world is moving forward, and Europe is still debating funding models and regional job quotas.

This merger changes nothing. Europe needs competition, not consolidation.

Since the talks became public, critics have framed this as a “European Master Plan”, a bureaucratic attempt to create a government-backed rival to SpaceX. That narrative might drive clicks, but it is misleading. This is not an EU-orchestrated industrial strategy. Airbus, not Brussels, initiated these talks, driven by market realities rather than state intervention.

So why are critics so quick to dismiss it? And why do the comparisons to SpaceX miss the point?

The ULA Comparison Is Flawed

In almost every single argument against the merger, three letters keep coming up. ULA.

For the uninformed, ULA stands for United Launch Alliance, an infamous joint venture between Lockheed and Boeing’s space launch operations that was forced upon the two companies by the US government after corruption scandals, the burst of the dot.com bubble, and legal battles between the two companies that threatened the future of the US domestic launch capabilities. A brief reading of the background shows that both companies had completely different philosophies on how to deliver the exact same services. Lockheed selected a ‘dirt cheap’ Russian engine for their Atlas program whereas Boeing’s Delta had the first large liquid-hydrogen/liquid-oxygen rocket engine developed in the US since the space shuttle. The companies appear to have polar opposite business strategies, ideas, etc.

Imagine Lockheed Martin and Boeing as two stubborn roommates, constantly arguing about who gets to use the TV remote and who left the dishes unwashed. Fed up, the US government handcuffed them together and made them co-manage the household. Instead of cleaning and organising, they spent their time arguing over methods and who is right.

It shouldn’t come as a surprise that the ULA merger is widely regarded as a failure and is often used as a warning against mergers. However, not all mergers share ULA’s fate. When market forces drive consolidation, space industry mergers can unlock innovation and sometimes even success.

Maxar, one of the world’s leading space technology companies, has a long history of strategic mergers that have shaped its position in the industry. Over the years, it has combined expertise in satellite imagery, robotics, and space infrastructure through acquisitions and consolidations. These mergers have enabled Maxar to expand its capabilities in Earth Observation and satellite communications, demonstrating how well-executed industry consolidation can enhance competitiveness and technological advancement.

In general, a merger’s success relies on a shared vision for the future, strong leadership, and most of all, whether it is willingly entered into. Without this foundation, even the most promising synergies can fall apart. However, with clearly defined goals and streamlined integration, mergers can foster growth.

ULA’s failure was a case of forced consolidation without a shared vision. But not all mergers are doomed to stagnation.

Airbus Has Done This Before

Unlike ULA, Airbus was not forced into an arranged marriage. It has spent decades using consolidation as a tool for growth rather than survival.

Airbus Defence and Space did not become Europe’s leading space company overnight. Its dominance is the result of decades of mergers and acquisitions, carefully integrating expertise from France, Germany, the UK, and Spain.

](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qf_V!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff610066e-c795-42fa-a348-d7b7c7800070_883x328.png)

Figure 1: A simplified view of how decades of aerospace mergers led to the formation of Airbus Defence and Space.

If this merger seems like a radical reshaping of Europe’s aerospace sector, it is not. Airbus, Thales, and Leonardo already work together on major projects, often in overlapping roles. Rather than smashing together three independent competitors, this move formalises what is already happening behind the scenes.

The companies have already been working together on high-profile programmes such as IRIS², the EU’s secure broadband constellation, and Galileo, the region’s answer to GPS. If anything, the merger is a belated recognition that these companies already rely on each other to keep Europe’s space infrastructure running.

Take Thales Alenia Space, where Thales owns 67 percent and Leonardo 33 percent. It is already one of Europe’s top satellite manufacturers, producing telecom, Earth observation, and navigation systems. Then there is Telespazio, another Thales-Leonardo joint venture focused on satellite services, secure communications, and ground infrastructure. Airbus already works closely with both, so the merger is not about creating monopolies.

This isn’t a shotgun wedding… it’s just making official what’s already happening.

Europe’s Airbus is No SpaceX… and That’s the Point

One of the more popular critiques of this merger is that it is Europe’s latest attempt to create its own version of SpaceX, a vertically integrated, fast-moving launch provider that can rival the United States. But that argument misunderstands both the nature of Airbus and the structure of Europe’s space industry.

SpaceX is a privately held company that integrates launch, satellite production, and broadband services under one roof. It thrives on rapid iteration, aggressive cost-cutting, and high-risk development cycles. Airbus, by contrast, is publicly traded, partially state-owned, and deeply embedded in European regulatory frameworks. Its business model is built on long-term contracts for defence, telecommunications, and scientific missions, not disruptive innovation.

This is not an attempt to build a European Starship or Starlink. The merger is about reducing redundancies, cutting procurement costs, and securing industrial scale for major European programs. Airbus has never been a serious competitor in the launch market, and its involvement in Arianespace remains secondary to its primary business of building high-reliability satellite platforms and defence technology.

What this merger can and cannot solve

Bringing together three of Europe’s largest aerospace firms will have significant effects, but not in the ways critics assume.

This merger is about efficiency. Airbus, Thales, and Leonardo already collaborate on major European projects, but overlapping responsibilities slow development. Consolidation could streamline operations, free up resources, and improve Europe’s competitiveness in the global space market. IRIS², Galileo, and Copernicus all require extensive collaboration between multiple companies, slowing development. A single, consolidated structure could reduce the bureaucratic inefficiencies that have plagued these programs for years.

Figure 2: Half of the IRIS² industrial base is already composed of Airbus, Thales, and Leonardo entities, highlighting their existing collaboration in Europe’s space sector.

Stronger industrial coordination could also improve Europe’s global competitiveness. A more unified industrial base could change that, particularly in defence-related space projects where European firms struggle to match the sheer spending power of the United States, which allocated over $26 billion to space programs in 2023 alone.

Merging Airbus, Thales, and Leonardo will not suddenly make ESA move faster. It will not fix Europe’s launch delays, nor will it create the conditions for a thriving commercial space sector. The merger does not change that reality.

If it collapsed tomorrow, it would not unlock venture capital for European space startups. It would not fix ESA’s painfully slow contract process, nor would it make European investors any less risk-averse. It does not force governments to rethink their reluctance to embrace a SpaceX-style model of rapid, venture-backed innovation.

The suggestion that Europe must decide between backing established industry leaders or fostering a dynamic NewSpace sector is a false choice. The reality is that Europe has already made its choice: it has spent decades propping up legacy aerospace firms while stifling commercial innovation.

At best, this consolidation makes an inefficient system slightly more efficient. At worst, it reinforces the same bureaucratic inertia that has held European aerospace back for decades.

This approach has led to cost overruns, inefficiencies, and delays. A report led by former ECB president Mario Draghi flagged geo-return as a major barrier to Europe’s space competitiveness, arguing that it stifles innovation and limits agility in a rapidly evolving industry. In response to mounting criticism, ESA has begun exploring reforms, but its entrenched procurement model remains a structural challenge.

EUSPA, the European Union’s Agency for the Space Programme, has only added more bureaucracy. Created to centralise European space policy, it has instead become an administrative extension of the European Commission. ## **What This Market Share Means for the Industry**

At first glance, the dominance of a few key players might seem like a sign of stagnation or lack of competition. However, the reality is more nuanced. These market leaders are not just holding their ground—they are continuing to evolve, setting the pace for the next phase of SATCOM innovation.

1.  **LEO Satellites Are Leading the Charge** The rise of **LEO satellite networks** is not just a trend; it’s a fundamental shift in the way global connectivity is provided. **Starlink**, as the largest player in this space, is leading the charge. Its rapid rollout of satellites is setting new expectations for connectivity.
    
2.  **Mergers Are Driving Consolidation, Not Competition** The **Viasat-Inmarsat** merger is a clear example of industry consolidation. While some might see this as an attempt to create a European alternative to **SpaceX's Starlink**, this merger isn’t about purely about creating a competitor; it’s about efficiency and increasing scale. It’s about bringing together capabilities that are already being shared across major projects like **IRIS²** and **Galileo**. Only time will tell if this consolidation is enough to compete, or whether these operators will continue to have their market share taken by Starlink.

These terminations appear to be part of a broader footprint reduction strategy, but little detail has been released publicly

*   A **NASA contract** with the **[University of Alaska Fairbanks](https://www.linkedin.com/school/university-of-alaska-fairbanks/)**, worth **$182,619**, was also terminated for convenience, again with a recorded savings of **$0**. *   A **NASA contract** with the **[National Society of Black Physicists](https://www.linkedin.com/company/nsbpinc/)**, valued at **$99,751**, was cancelled with a savings of **$0**. The project involved organising a Student Leadership Development Summit (SLDS) and topical workshops to advance engagement in planetary science.
    
*   A **NASA contract** with **[Virginia Tech](https://www.linkedin.com/school/virginia-tech/)** for **$763,904** was terminated, showing **no savings**. This interdisciplinary project aimed to democratise data for adaptation decision-making in the North-Atlantic Coastal Plain, focusing on hazards like land subsidence and compound flooding.
    
*   A **NASA contract** with **[John Hopkins University](https://www.linkedin.com/company/john-hopkins-university/)**, valued at **$969,349**, was also terminated with no financial savings. This project focused on resolving intra-urban variability in heat and air quality from space and ground observations to support environmental justice initiatives.
    
*   A **NASA contract** with **Chenega Global Protection, LLC**, valued at **$231,345**, was cancelled under a Termination for Convenience Agreement. The project had provided security police officer support for NASA's Earth Information Center (EIC) but was terminated without any savings recorded.
    
*   A **NASA contract** with **[George Mason University](https://www.linkedin.com/school/george-mason-university/)**, valued at **$529,129**, was cancelled, again reporting no savings. The project addressed disparities in health and safety effects of dust storms across the United States under NASA's interdisciplinary research in earth sciences programme.
    
*   A **NASA contract** with **[Brown University](https://www.linkedin.com/school/brown-university/)**, worth **$752,680**, was cancelled without generating any recorded savings. The project focused on using NASA Earth observations to support resilient community planning around California’s Salton Sea.
    
*   A **NASA contract** with the **[Natural Areas Conservancy](https://www.linkedin.com/company/natural-areas-conservancy/)**, valued at **$485,603**, was cancelled with no savings. The project assessed access to nature and related benefits in environmental justice communities across US cities.
    
*   A **NASA contract** with **[Cornell University](https://www.linkedin.com/school/cornell-university/)**, valued at **$260,000**, was cancelled with a savings of **$0**. The contract supported an innovative workshop on Equity, Diversity, Inclusion, and Accessibility (EDIA) for leaders in planetary science.
    
*   A **NASA contract** with **[NUBURU® Inc.](https://www.linkedin.com/company/nuburu/)**, worth **$849,989**, was cancelled without any financial savings. The project aimed to develop blue laser technology for planetary and lunar power management under an SBIR Phase II effort.
    
*   A **NASA contract** with **[Unibap AB](https://www.linkedin.com/company/unibap/)**, worth **$70,000**, was terminated with no savings. The project involved development of the OSE-SAT in-space autonomy testbed.
    
*   A **NASA contract** with the **[UCAR - The University Corporation for Atmospheric Research](https://www.linkedin.com/company/university-corporation-for-atmospheric-research/)**, valued at **$14,000**, was terminated without savings. The project was linked to the DYNAMIC-X Phase A study focused on dynamical atmosphere-ionosphere coupling.
    
*   A **NASA contract** with **R3 UNIQ Inc**, valued at **$71,649**, was cancelled with no recorded savings. This project supported licenses and maintenance for the OMNeT network simulation software system.
    

None of these projects recorded any savings according to the DOGE database, raising major questions about how terminations are being counted and reported.

NebuLink will continue tracking space-related cuts as they appear on the DOGE API. This is just the start of a longer series. Our goal is to turn government transparency into real accountability, highlighting not just what was cut, but also what was lost.

**[Capella Space](https://www.linkedin.com/company/capellaspace/)**, the poster-child of commercial SAR, just agreed to a $311 million all-stock takeover by **[IonQ](https://www.linkedin.com/company/ionq-co/)**, a quantum-computing firm now bent on building a space-based “quantum internet” for defence customers. On paper the match looks tidy: Capella supplies flight-proven satellites; IonQ brings quantum networking tech amassed through a recent buying spree.

Reality is messier. Capella’s buses are optimised for rapid radar imaging, huge panels, hot duty cycles, and kilowatts of RF, everything a Quantum Key Distribution payload dislikes. No entangled-photon source, cryogenic detector, or fine-pointing system comes with the deal.

Thanks for reading NebuLink: The Business of Space ! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Pull it off and IonQ fields the first U.S. commercial QKD constellation, tapping defence, cloud-security, and sovereign-crypto budgets. Miss the mark and a once-leading Earth-observation company becomes collateral damage.

## **What does Capella do?**

I suspect most of my readers are familiar with Capella, but for those not in the know Capella is, first and foremost, a synthetic-aperture-radar (SAR) data company. Its satellites transmit pulses toward the Earth and measure the echoes. Because radar penetrates cloud, smoke and darkness, SAR delivers imagery-and-measurement products on any continent, at any time of day, in any weather, capabilities optical-camera constellations simply cannot match.

Capella then processes the raw data into a useable format, creating a variety of output types ranging from simple spotlight images, through to integrated dashboards complimented with fancy machine learning techniques to provide persistent intelligence. This is used by everyone from commercial operators monitoring supply chains, to militaries to monitor troop movements.

[

![Article content](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/0d3822dc-4c90-4617-8721-a73897c3e1d1_1488x837.png "Article content")



](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Th0V!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0d3822dc-4c90-4617-8721-a73897c3e1d1_1488x837.png)

An image captured by Capella of a spaceport launch pad and assembly area in China, showcasing the capabilities of SAR imagery.

## **So what is a space-based QKD system anyway?**

I’ll admit, quantum is not my strongest area. It always sounds like magic to me. It is one of those buzzwords that is thrown about that I think most people nod and smile at. However, after reading a lot of articles and asking some dear friends very stupid questions, here’s my best explanation for a non-technical audience, feel free to comment why this is wrong below.

### **Why quantum?**

_Imagine a general dispatching vital battle orders through hostile territory. Tradition calls for sealing the scroll with the regiment’s unique wax stamp: if that seal is still pristine when the courier arrives, the officers can execute the plan, certain no spy has pried inside; if it is cracked, they scrap the orders and rethink. Yet counter-intelligence eventually masters perfect counterfeit stamps, making even the finest wax seal untrustworthy._

_To outwit the forgers, the general adds a modern twist: he bonds a colour-change security label across the flap, much like the stickers shippers use to show mishandling. This label stays clear as long as the scroll remains closed but flashes bright red the instant the seal is lifted, and it can never return to clear. Now the officers have a tamper check that no enemy can reset: scroll delivered with a clear window, orders are safe; window turned red, the plan is compromised and must be revised._

[

![Article content](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/b3ebd408-c6df-4ed2-90a2-d144d5186d4b_400x222.jpeg "Article content")



](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FS3L!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb3ebd408-c6df-4ed2-90a2-d144d5186d4b_400x222.jpeg)

An example of a colour-changing TiltWatch indicator: green when untouched, red once tipped, providing a permanent, tamper-evident signal..

Think of that label as the stand-in for a quantum seal. Just as the window flips irreversibly from green to red when someone tilts the package, a photon’s quantum state flips irreversibly if anyone tries to measure it in flight. The colour change tells the receiver, '_This parcel was handled; trust nothing inside_.'

In quantum key distribution the changed photon tells Alice and Bob, '_Someone saw this; discard this key._” In both cases the security comes not from trusting the courier, or the math behind a wax stamp, but from an unforgeable physical reaction that instantly exposes tampering.

### **So why space?**

These systems are already being deployed on the ground, however, current land infrastructure relies on fibre-optic links, with repeaters every few hundred kilometers. Operators must insert a repeater station, or, more commonly today, a “trusted node", every few hundred kilometres.

Each node is a bunker full of optics and security personnel that must be certified, guarded and, above all, trusted not to copy the keys it handles. Build a continent-spanning link and you introduce dozens of such trust points, each a potential insider threat, diplomatic sticking point, or multimillion-dollar facilities bill. If you wanted to have a secure quantum comms system from the South China Sea through to the US West Coast, you'd need at least 50 intermediate nodes, all across the ocean and potentially hostile land.

This is where space-based QKD comes in. Instead of having to have a repeater every 100km, instead you'd have the photons directly beamed between destinations with only the satellite infrastructure in between. A space-based system allows a single entity to be in control of the entire system, from start to finish.

### **IonQ, who are they and what have they been buying?**

IonQ is a Maryland start-up that turns individual atoms into qubits and sells cloud access to its quantum computers. Lately it has shifted from “just make the processor” to “own the whole quantum-secure network,” buying whatever pieces it still needs.

**Its shopping list so far in just a few months...**

1.  **January 2025 – Qubitekk (≈ USD 22 million).** Added hardware for entanglement distribution and more than one hundred quantum-network patents.
    
2.  **February 2025 – ID Quantique (≈ USD 250 million).** Brought in the long-time leader in quantum-safe encryption chips and single-photon detectors.
    
3.  **Early May 2025 – Lightsynq Technologies (price undisclosed).** Secured photonic-memory and quantum-repeater intellectual property that will be essential for scaling any global QKD network.
    
4.  **Mid-May 2025 – Capella Space (≈ USD 311 million, all-stock).** Marked IonQ’s first purchase of substantial physical assets in orbit, giving it an operational satellite fleet and classified U.S. government clearances.
    

Put together, that stack now covers chips, detectors, repeaters, and, with Capella, the spacecraft, to run a future quantum-secure communications network.

### **Are Capella's SAR buses actually any good for QKD?**

Think of Capella’s satellites as sports cars: built to dart from one target to the next so they can snap radar pictures for paying customers. A quantum-key mission, by contrast, wants a meditation cushion. To keep a laser beam locked on a ground telescope, the spacecraft must hold itself rock-steady; even a tiny wiggle can ruin the key. Capella’s “sports car” bus jitters a little every time it whips its radar dish around which is fine for imaging, fatal for single photons.

The radar gear brings two more headaches. First, it blasts out radio waves strong enough to swamp the ultrasensitive detectors a quantum experiment needs. Second, it dumps a lot of heat during each imaging pass, while quantum optics like a calm, very cold environment. Add the fact that the big radar antenna hogs an entire side of the satellite, leaving almost no room for the mirrors and telescopes a quantum payload would require, and you can see why the fit is awkward. I would love to be in the room when the engineers get told about these requirements, but I'd hate to be the one telling them.

So why bother? Because the platform itself is already space-proven and cleared for classified US missions. Its thrusters, batteries and fault-protection code have flight heritage the Pentagon trusts, saving IonQ years of paperwork. Strap a prototype quantum box onto a few of Capella’s later satellites and IonQ can gather real-world data on vibration, radio noise and temperature swings, information it needs before designing a purpose-built “quiet” quantum bus. In short, the radar fleet isn’t the final vehicle, but it’s a cheap, government-approved test track that gets IonQ into orbit fast, not to mention the manufacturing and existing tech development.

### **Who Else Is Playing the Quantum-Keys-from-Space Game?**

If IonQ jumps into orbit tomorrow it won’t be alone; several heavy-hitters are already circling the field.

*   **China** Beijing sent _Micius_ up in 2016, beamed entangled photons over 1,200 km and has been polishing the tech ever since.
    
*   **Europe:** ESA and SES are building **Eagle-1**, a geostationary “trusted-node” satellite that should launch late next year. It won’t wow on distance like _Micius_, but Europe is all about standards, interoperability and making sure every member state can plug in.
    
*   **Canada:** The Canadian Space Agency’s **QEYSSat** heads to low-Earth orbit in 2025. It’s a pure science mission, modest budget, solid engineering, lots of papers to follow, good for proving measurements, not for selling commercial keys just yet.
    
*   **Singapore & Spain:** **SpeQtral** (Singapore) has two microsats on the drawing board, backed by its national space office, while **Thales Alenia Space + Hispasat** pitch a Spanish GEO platform under the PERTE Aeroespacial fund.
    

Put IonQ in that mix and you get a clear picture: it could be the **only US commercial player** with metal already in orbit, but it’s jumping in mid-race. China has years of flight data, Europe has a GEO bird nearly ready, and IonQ doesn’t yet have an entanglement payload on-orbit. The company’s edge is speed, buying Capella skips the “how do we get a satellite licence?” stage, but it will need to sprint on hardware development to catch the veterans.

### **What’s Still Missing, and What It’ll Cost**

Buying Capella gets IonQ a ride to orbit, but not the quantum magic itself. Here’s the short version of the to-do list:

*   **A lightbulb that makes entangled photons.** Right now (i think) IonQ has zero flight-qualified “quantum lightbulbs.” Designing one that survives launch shaking and radiation is a multi-year, multi-million-dollar project.
    
*   **Rock-steady pointing gear.** Those single photons must hit a ground telescope the size of a dustbin lid from 600 km up. That means fine-steering mirrors that twitch thousands of times a second and attitude sensors a hundred times more precise than Capella’s.
    
*   **Deep-freeze detectors.** The best single-photon sensors run at a few kelvin. Cramming cryocoolers and vibration dampers into a smallsat bus is tricky (and heavy on power).
    
*   **A cloud-dodging ground network.** Quantum links die in fog and thick cloud, so IonQ needs a global ring of optical stations in desert-dry spots,( think Atacama, Canary Islands, Namibia) plus fibre back-haul to data centres. Building or leasing that real estate is easily nine figures.
    
*   **A LEO relay mesh.** There needs to be a dedicated low-orbit backbone to ferry keys from one satellite to the next until a clear ground site appears. Building that mesh means dozens of extra spacecraft or a pricey capacity lease from the SDA’s optical network, or from someone like **[Amazon Project Kuiper](https://www.linkedin.com/showcase/amazon-project-kuiper/)**, **[SpaceX](https://www.linkedin.com/company/spacex/)**, or **[Kepler Communications Inc.](https://www.linkedin.com/company/kepler-communications-inc-/)**.
    
*   **Probably a GEO relay.** Pure LEO coverage leaves gaps. A single micro-GEO satellite can store keys and trickle them down 24/7, but a GEO bird with quantum kit runs well past €150 m (see ESA’s Eagle-1 budget).
    
*   **Regulators and laser staff.** Every laser beam that crosses an air route needs safety clearance; every cryptographic export needs paperwork. Multiply that by 50+ countries and you see the admin cliff.
    

Put a rough price tag on all that and you’re staring at **US $500 million or more** before the first paying customer signs up. In other words, IonQ has bought itself a fast start, not a finished product.

### **Opportunity versus Risk: What IonQ Stands to Gain and Lose**

**Why the gamble looks tempting.** If IonQ stitches the missing pieces together, it can sell quantum-secure keys the way satellite operators once sold minutes of voice or megabits of bandwidth, only at far higher margins. Defence agencies want links that neither hackers nor future AI code-breakers can quietly record and decrypt later. Capella’s existing clearances give IonQ a fast lane into classified US budgets, and a dual-use satellite that collects SAR images while handing out unbreakable keys would command premium tasking fees from intelligence customers who value both data types on the same secure pipe.

**Where the tripwires lie.** Every upside has a mirror hazard. The hardware schedule could slip past 2028, by which time terrestrial fibre networks with quantum repeaters may cover enough ground to blunt the “only in space” argument. Export-control regimes might classify entangled-photon sources as munitions, bottling IonQ inside US borders just as customers abroad open their wallets. China, already flying entanglement payloads, could undercut IonQ’s pricing or hand subsidised keys to Belt-and-Road allies, eroding market share before IonQ’s first node is fully online. And looming over everything is execution complexity: folding Qubitekk, ID Quantique, Lightsynq and Capella into one programme while turning a radar bus into a quantum relay is a management gauntlet that has humbled bigger aerospace names.

**Bottom line for investors and customers.** Pull it off and IonQ owns the first commercial, end-to-end quantum-secure backbone in orbit. Miss a step and the company could burn through half a billion dollars only to watch state-funded rivals win the market, or see its own integration timetable drown in culture clashes and regulatory red tape. The bet is bold, the window narrow, and the payoff potentially transformative for every network that still depends on encryption mathematics ageing fast in the shadow of quantum computing.

### **Conclusion, The Very Long Road Ahead**

Buying Capella is IonQ’s boldest move yet, but it is only a down-payment on a globe-spanning quantum network. The company now is set to own an accredited satellite fleet and a shortcut through the regulatory jungle, yet it still faces a long climb in photonics, cryogenics and ground infrastructure. Whether that shortcut outweighs the engineering mountain remains to be seen.

However, I’ve paused the analysis here; the next instalment will tackle the deal from Capella’s side of the table. Given IonQ’s long-term focus on quantum networking and the engineering clashes between radar and QKD, **there’s a very real possibility that “Capella 2.0” won’t be flying SAR satellites at all.**

164203257.How Much Does It Really Cost To Launch

A quick case study that cuts launch costs in half just by swapping out obsolete space hardware. No redesigns, no hype, just updated assumptions.

## **The economics of putting a data centre in space**

I recently came across a post estimating what it would take to launch a top-end AI rack, specifically the **[NVIDIA](https://www.linkedin.com/company/nvidia/)** GB200 NVL72, into orbit. The author walked through the power draw, cooling requirements, and launch cost, concluding that it would cost around 20 million dollars just to get it up there.

Thanks for reading NebuLink: The Business of Space ! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

At first glance, the numbers looked reasonable. But the assumptions were built around 1990s space hardware. The post used ISS solar arrays, legacy ammonia radiators, and made no attempt to update the architecture for what is available today. That got me thinking. What if we ran the same problem using current-generation systems?

This article is a case study. I keep the rack constant and only swap out the outdated power and thermal systems. Even with that limited change, the launch mass drops by half and the cost comes down by over 10 million dollars. And that is before we address the rack itself, which, as I will explain later, is completely unsuited to orbital deployment.

Let’s run the numbers.

## **This Is Not Just a Thought Experiment**

This is a problem worth solving, because this is no longer a speculative topic. China has already begun deploying its **Star Compute** constellation, integrating onboard AI models into a massive distributed space-based network. **[Axiom Space](https://www.linkedin.com/company/axiom-space/)** is preparing to deploy on-orbit data processing nodes aboard **[Kepler Communications Inc.](https://www.linkedin.com/company/kepler-communications-inc-/)**, starting with a test deployment and eventually building its own orbital data centres. **[Starcloud](https://www.linkedin.com/company/starcloudinc/)**, a Y Combinator-backed company, has raised tens of millions of dollars to build orbital data centres, with a demonstrator flight scheduled to launch this summer. New entrants like **[Sophia Space](https://www.linkedin.com/company/sophia-space/)** are appearing almost monthly.

This is not a theoretical debate about the future. It is a present-day race to operationalise orbital compute. Which is why it is important to get the numbers right.

## **Where the $20 Million Figure Came From**

The original post was a rough estimate of what it would take to launch a high-performance data centre rack into orbit. The author chose the NVIDIA GB200 NVL72, assumed a power draw of around 120 kilowatts, and worked out the mass needed for solar arrays and cooling using International Space Station hardware as a reference. Then they multiplied the total mass by Falcon 9 launch costs and arrived at a price tag of about $20 million.

At a high level, here is what the post assumed:

*   **Rack:** 3,000 pounds (about 1,360 kilograms)
    
*   **Power system:** Four ISS Solar Array Wings, each producing 31 kilowatts and weighing 2,500 pounds. That adds up to 10,000 pounds or 4,536 kilograms.
    
*   **Cooling:** Two ammonia-loop radiators from the ISS External Active Thermal Control System, with a combined weight of 3,300 pounds or 1,500 kilograms.
    
*   **Total mass:** 7,396 kilograms
    
*   **Launch cost:** 2,645 dollars per kilogram
    
*   **Total cost:** Just under $19.6 million
    

To be fair, the maths checks out if you accept the assumptions. But that is exactly the problem. The assumptions are tied to technology designed in the 1990s. None of these systems reflect what is available in 2025. And once you swap them out, the economics shift completely.

## **Power: Why 4,500 Kilograms is the Wrong Starting Point**

The ISS Solar Array Wings, or SAWs, are a common reference point in space power discussions. They are large, visible, and historically proven. But they are also outdated. Designed in the 1990s, these arrays used rigid panel structures, early gallium arsenide cells, and heavy deployment trusses. Their specific power is about **27 watts per kilogram**, or **12.4 watts per pound**. That might have been fine when launch cost was 50,000 dollars per kilogram, but it makes little sense today.

If you are building a power system in 2025, this is the wrong place to start.

### **Upgrade 1: iROSA, Already in Orbit**

Redwire’s iROSA system is a modern roll-out blanket array, now deployed on the ISS. It delivers far better power-to-weight performance. Each unit provides 20 kilowatts and weighs about 340 kilograms, which gives a specific power of around 58.8 watts per kilogram.

To power a 120 kilowatt system using iROSA, you would need about six units, which adds up to around 2,040 kilograms of solar arrays. That is already less than half the mass of the original SAW-based estimate.

### **Upgrade 2: Redwire’s Current-Generation Arrays**

According to Redwire’s datasheet, their newest roll-out arrays deliver 120 watts per kilogram. Using this, you would only need 1,000 kilograms of array mass to generate 120 kilowatts.

That brings the required solar mass down by over 3,500 kilograms compared to the legacy design. And this is not theoretical. These arrays are commercially available and being actively marketed.

### **Looking Ahead to 2030**

By 2030, solar technologies are expected to reach 200 watts per kilogram. This is driven by advances in thin-film photovoltaics, lighter structural materials, and the possibility of in-orbit assembly.

At that level of performance, you would only need 600 kilograms of solar array mass to power a 120 kilowatt compute rack. That is a reduction of 87 percent compared to the ISS-era baseline.

### **Why This Matters**

Reducing the power system mass from 4,500 kilograms to 1,000 or even 600 changes the economics completely. It does not just save money. It opens up the ability to co-launch with other systems, to scale deployments, and to rethink how orbital compute infrastructure is designed.

And this is before we look at cooling.

## **Cooling: Why 1,500 Kilograms is Also Too Much**

Once you have power, the next challenge is thermal rejection. A rack like the NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 draws about 120 kilowatts of power, and in space, almost all of that becomes waste heat. Unlike on Earth, you cannot rely on fans, airflow, or coolant loops venting into the atmosphere. In orbit, heat must be moved using fluid loops or heat pipes and then radiated away into space.

The original post referenced the ISS External Active Thermal Control System, which uses ammonia loop radiators. Each loop is quoted at 1,500 kilograms to reject 70 kilowatts. You would need two of them to manage 120 kilowatts, so the assumed radiator mass was 3,300 pounds, or roughly 1,500 kilograms.

Again, this system was built for a different mission. The ISS cooling setup was designed with full redundancy, large fixed radiators, and the ability to work across all orbital attitudes with a crew on board. None of that applies to a self-contained, purpose-built compute node.

### **Modern Options: Already More Efficient**

Thermal systems available in 2025 are significantly lighter. High-performance deployable radiators now achieve between 100 and 120 watts per kilogram. These are used on large satellites, space stations, and spacecraft, and are typically based on roll-out structures, loop heat pipes, or pumped two-phase systems.

If we take a conservative figure of 106 watts per kilogram, you would only need **1,132 kilograms** of radiator mass to reject 120 kilowatts of heat. That is already **400 kilograms lighter** than the ISS-based design.

### **Looking Ahead to 2030**

Future radiator systems are targeting **200 watts per kilogram**, especially for larger orbital platforms where mass and surface area efficiency become even more critical.

At 200 watts per kilogram, the required radiator mass drops to just **600 kilograms**. That is a saving of **900 kilograms** compared to the original estimate, and a **60 percent improvement** over today’s best available systems.

These newer systems are not just lighter. They are also more modular, easier to stow for launch, and faster to deploy once in orbit. They simplify thermal architecture, reduce mechanical complexity, and make it easier to scale up.

Sub-metre satellite imagery was once the exclusive domain of government agencies. This premise has been upended by massive industry shifts where today, anyone with a credit card can task a satellite. This has begun to revolutionise industries across the world, from corporate intelligence to disaster response, however, this revolution also arms a far more sinister clientele: terrorists and militaries

From Kashmir’s Pahalgam through to Khartoum’s neighbourhoods, todays commercial space operators have become unwilling participants in terror attacks and troop movements. This article today explores the use cases.

# Case Studies

## **1\. Russian Missile Strikes in Ukraine (February–December 2022)**

Between February and December 2022, The [Atlantic’s Graeme Wood](https://www.theatlantic.com/international/archive/2024/03/american-satellites-russia-ukraine-war/677775/) identified a striking pattern: more than 350 instances in which commercial satellite images of Ukrainian sites were purchased just days before those same locations were hit by Russian missile strikes. Journalists noted that these taskings spanned deep into Ukrainian territory, far beyond frontline areas, and raised the question of whether ostensibly civilian imagery feeds were being repurposed for targeting.

[Molfar analysis](https://molfar.com/en/blog/chy-kupuyut-rosiyany-v-maxar-i-planet-foto-shchob-obstrilyuvaty-ukrainu?utm_source=chatgpt.com) set out to verify this claim by examining 321 confirmed Russian strikes from 24 February to 31 December 2022. They found that in 277 cases, over 85 percent, the exact target area had indeed been imaged one to two days before impact, covering bridges, ammunition depots and defensive positions around Kharkiv and Mykolaiv. By routing orders through intermediary brokers and shell companies, planners bypassed export controls and obtained sub-metre data for under USD 500 per scene, materially sharpening strike precision.

To test how easily these taskings could slip through vetting, Molfar’s HUMINT team posed as foreign buyers and approached several Maxar and Planet resellers. Despite sanctions and corporate policies prohibiting sales to sanctioned actors, some distributors offered imagery with minimal identity checks, demonstrating how intermediaries can enable access to sensitive data even when primary providers deny direct sales. This finding lays bare the ethical blind spot in today’s open satellite marketplaces and underscores the urgent need for tighter end-use controls.

## **2\. Houthi Attacks on Red Sea Shipping (October 2024)**

In April 2025, the [Financial Times reported that Chang Guang Satellite Technology Co. Ltd, a commercial Chinese satellite firm with deep ties to the People’s Liberation Army, was supplying near-real-time imagery to Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen](https://www.ft.com/content/628b404b-2a24-4853-8f3c-9caad408ef8f). According to U.S. officials cited by the FT, Chang Guang’s commercial division routed sub-metre optical and radar data through Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, enabling the Houthis to monitor U.S. and allied naval movements in the southern Red Sea with unprecedented clarity.

A [Wall Street Journal investigation](https://www.wsj.com/world/china/the-chinese-satellite-firm-washington-accuses-of-helping-u-s-foes-b5e68d2e) added that these brokered feeds were augmented by commercial vessel-tracking services, which together improved the rebels’ hit probability by over 30 percent compared to unguided attacks. The WSJ detailed how Houthi planners used precise geospatial updates, sourced via Russian intermediaries and Chang Guang’s imagery, to synchronise missile and drone launches against both merchant ships and naval vessels, turning ostensibly civilian data into battlefield-grade targeting intelligence.

In response to rising concerns, the [European Commission and ESA have begun deliberately degrading or delaying public Sentinel-2 coverage over the Red Sea corridor](https://hntrbrk.com/eu-satellites/). Sentinel-2’s high-resolution, multispectral imagery is temporarily withheld for 24–48-hour periods in critical zones, a move officials say aligns with “applicable regulations and operational considerations” and aims to deny hostile actors unfettered access to real-time monitoring feeds. This new restriction marks one of the first instances in which an open-data programme has been selectively throttled to protect maritime traffic from precision-guided threats.

## **3\. Pahalgam Ambush in Jammu & Kashmir, (April 2025)**

Between 2 February and 12 April, [tasking requests for sub-metre imagery of Pahalgam more than doubled on Maxar’s portal](https://theprint.in/defence/pahalgam-satellite-image-us-space-tech-firm-maxar-technologies/2620666/), with a dozen separate orders zeroing in on the town’s roads, hotels and valley overlooks. The final request arrived on 12 April, ten days before terrorists opened fire on a tourist convoy in Baisaran Valley, killing twenty-six civilians.

Early reports linked the surge in orders to Maxar’s former partner, Pakistan-linked Business Systems International. Within hours of that claim, Maxar removed BSI from its list of resellers and issued a categorical denial. An [India Today TV report](https://www.indiatoday.in/india/story/maxar-satellite-experts-imagery-pahalgam-terror-attack-india-pak-conflict-terrorists-2723622-2025-05-12) quoted a Maxar spokesperson: “Our records indicate that BSI has neither placed any tasking orders over Pahalgam or the surrounding areas this year, nor ordered any imagery through our archive.” Intelligence analysts echoed that local sleeper-cell support and readily available public maps made high-end taskings unnecessary for an ambush carried out at point-blank range.

Geospatial experts, including ASPI’s Nathan Ruser, found no abnormal imaging patterns. Ruser noted that on-demand imagery markets have expanded to include dozens of global providers and mobile-app ordering, so spikes alone do not prove malicious intent. Still, the timing and focus of these twelve taskings remain striking. Whether driven by curiosity, research or reconnaissance, even if they didn’t supply those images, the fact that taskings occurred so shortly before the attack underscores the ethical blind spot in today’s open satellite marketplaces.

## **4\. National governments are worried about easing restrictions (2001, 2020)**

Governments maintain ultimate control over high-resolution commercial imagery through a mix of licensing, resolution caps and “shutter control” provisions that date back decades. In the United States, the Land Remote Sensing Policy Act of 1992 requires NOAA licenses for any domestic satellite operator, and grants the executive branch authority to deny or delay image collection over sensitive areas. Rather than invoke formal shutter closures, Washington has typically employed what critics call “checkbook shutter control”—purchasing exclusive rights to imagery instead. After 9/11, for example, the [Pentagon bought sole access to all Ikonos satellite pictures of Afghanistan from Space Imaging](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2001/oct/17/physicalsciences.afghanistan), blocking civilian and media outlets from viewing detailed post-strike scenes without any public legal order to do so .

In July 2020, [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/article/world/israel-feels-exposed-as-us-drops-satellite-imaging-cap-idUSKBN2470VD/) reported that the US eased restrictions under the Kyl–Bingaman Amendment to allow American satellite firms to sell imagery of Israel and the Palestinian territories at resolutions up to 0.4 m, down from the previous 2 m limit. A senior Israeli Defence Ministry official warned that such high-resolution data could be exploited by terrorist groups like Hezbollah and Hamas to pinpoint both military installations and civilian infrastructure for rocket attacks and sabotage. Despite assurances that foreign providers already offer sub-2 m imagery, Israel has urged renewed scrutiny of end-use policies to prevent its enemies from gaining a precision-strike advantage.

# Policies

## **Why Existing Safeguards Have Fallen Short**

These cases share three systemic gaps:

1.  **Intermediary Opacity**  
    Shell companies and geospatial brokers obscure true end users, leaving providers unaware of ultimate intent.
    
2.  **Marketplace Blindspots**  
    On-demand portals lack real-time anomaly detection. Repeated taskings over sensitive sites sail through unflagged.
    
3.  **Regulatory Loopholes**  
    Export controls focus on satellite hardware transfers, not downstream data distribution once imagery is in orbit.
    

The result is a buyer’s market for targeting intelligence: minimal marginal cost per image, yet decisive tactical gains.

## **Existing Safeguards**

Before we can close the ethical gap, it helps to understand the measures already in place:

1.  **Provider Vetting & End-Use Declarations**  
    Commercial imagery firms require new customers to complete Know-Your-Customer checks and sign end-use agreements attesting they will not resell data to sanctioned or prohibited actors. Many also screen orders against embargoed-area lists and maintain internal compliance teams to flag suspicious taskings.
    
2.  **Export-Control Regimes**  
    In the US, the Land Remote Sensing Policy Act (1992) mandates NOAA licences for any domestic satellite operator and empowers “shutter control” to deny or delay collection over specified sites. The Kyl–Bingaman Amendment further caps U.S. providers’ spatial resolution at 2 m (recently eased to 0.4 m) for imagery over Israel and the Palestinian territories. Similar licensing frameworks exist, albeit less uniformly in Europe and Australia.
    
3.  **Shutter & “Checkbook” Controls**  
    While formal shutter closures are rare, governments often purchase exclusive tasking rights to sensitive areas (e.g. U.S. take-rights to Ikonos imagery after 9/11) to keep high-resolution data off the open market. This “checkbook shutter” approach can be faster and less visible than regulatory bans.

1.  **Transparent Tasking Metadata Feeds**

Commercial satellite imagery underpins critical civilian and humanitarian applications, but its dual-use nature demands a recalibrated approach. By embracing transparency, automation, international cooperation and independent oversight, the industry can preserve the promise of on-demand Earth observation while denying adversaries the means to turn those same pixels into precision strikes.

The time to act is now.

1. Russian Missile Strikes in Ukraine (February–December 2022)

Between February and December 2022, The Atlantic’s Graeme Wood identified a striking pattern: more than 350 instances in which commercial satellite images of Ukrainian sites were purchased just days before those same locations were hit by Russian missile strikes. Journalists noted that these taskings spanned deep into Ukrainian territory, far beyond frontline areas, and raised the question of whether ostensibly civilian imagery feeds were being repurposed for targeting.

Molfar analysis set out to verify this claim by examining 321 confirmed Russian strikes from 24 February to 31 December 2022. They found that in 277 cases, over 85 percent, the exact target area had indeed been imaged one to two days before impact, covering bridges, ammunition depots and defensive positions around Kharkiv and Mykolaiv. Between 2 February and 12 April, tasking requests for sub-metre imagery of Pahalgam more than doubled on Maxar’s portal, with a dozen separate orders zeroing in on the town’s roads, hotels and valley overlooks. # Why the ISS Retirement Changes Everything

The retirement of the ISS marks the end of the era of government-owned and operated human spaceflight infrastructure in LEO. This transition is not driven by technical or commercial demand, but by policy and procurement priorities. Governments no longer wish to carry the long-term operational burden of orbital platforms.

In response, a wave of commercial space station ventures has emerged, often with government backing. However, these projects risk reproducing the same structural issues that challenged the ISS: high costs, bespoke infrastructure, limited accessibility, and ongoing dependence on public subsidy.

This paper evaluates the foundations of the ISS model and proposes alternative approaches informed by adjacent sectors. It argues that future space stations must function either as modular service platforms or as equity-sharing ventures embedded in the success of onboard activities. These models, coupled with transitional public funding and global buy-in, offer a scalable path toward sustainable orbital infrastructure.

# Why the ISS Model is Flawed

## A broken funding formala

While the ISS has delivered scientific, technical, and diplomatic value, its cost structure is fundamentally unsustainable. NASA recovers <5% of operating costs from commercial users. The majority of funding comes from US taxpayers, with modest contributions from international partners. As public budgets tighten and political focus shifts, this model is no longer viable. Agencies now look to commercial industry, not just to supplement ISS capabilities, but to replace them entirely, without a proven economic blueprint for doing so.

## Bespoke, one of a kind, and costly

Despite lower launch costs, orbital infrastructure remains prohibitively expensive due to its design philosophy. Current stations are still bespoke, human-rated systems, each with unique hardware, integration requirements, and operational constraints. This makes them slow to build, costly to maintain, and difficult to scale. The contrast within the space sector is instructive: standardised buses, COTS components, and batch production are dramatically cutting costs elsewhere. Until orbital infrastructure is treated as a product, not a prototype, commercialisation is out of reach.

## Space tourism won’t pay the bills

Space tourism is touted as a solution, but it offers limited economic value. The addressable market is small, highly price-sensitive, and not designed for repeat business, often structured as prestige experiences, one-time ticket sales to a narrow group of individuals, rather than recurring infrastructure use.

## The limits of research revenue

Research holds value, but it cannot sustain a space station. Most research demand is publicly funded, one-off, and has limited opportunity for repeat business. This model, selling access, offers insufficient volume to support permanent infrastructure. Without an industrial base, research cannot provide the revenue needed to replace government subsidies.

# Does this problem exist in other industries?

Despite what everyone tells you, space isn’t that special and unique. For example, both biotechnology and advanced manufacturing, providers confront the same barriers that face commercial space stations: massive upfront capital requirements, specialised hardware integration and a fragmented customer base of small, under-funded innovators.

Yet these sectors have overcome those hurdles by productising access and sharing risk and reward with their users, but how?

In **biotech** incubators such as Johnson & Johnson’s JLABS or Ginkgo Bioworks’ Foundry, infrastructure providers do far more than lease space. They offer bundled services including laboratory equipment, regulatory guidance and business development support, often reducing or waiving bench fees in exchange for a 5 to 10% equity stake or a royalty on future product sales. This model aligns incentives by sharing downside risk with cash-strapped startups and participating directly in upside when a therapy wins FDA approval or a synthetic biology product enters commercial production.

Similarly, advanced manufacturing ecosystems such as Protolabs’ on-demand CNC and 3D printing services and the Fraunhofer Institutes’ pilot production lines combine standardised tooling, rapid prototyping and quality certification into a manufacturing-as-a-service offering. Clients pay predictable per-part fees rather than investing capital in bespoke machinery, while providers amortise their platforms across multiple users. In both industries, productised access, transparent pricing and shared-risk investment lower entry barriers, accelerate time to market and transform fixed-cost facilities into scalable, value-generating platforms. Commercial space stations must adopt the same playbook.

# Two business models for sustainable space stations

Now that we know how other industries have solved it, let’s translate this into specific models for space.

## Platform-as-a-Service for Orbit

To eliminate access friction and turn microgravity into a repeatable service, a commercial station must be productised end-to-end. Rather than bespoke, one-off missions, operators need to offer:

1.  **Standardised Modules** that any payload can plug into without custom integration
    
2.  **Transparent, Usage-Based Pricing** per kilogram, per week or per experiment type
    
3.  **Pre-Defined Integration Pathways** with set SLAs for payload delivery, launch windows and on-station support
    

This could be used in pharmaceutical R&D, advanced materials testing and in-orbit manufacturing trials. By treating microgravity like a utility, customers gain predictable turnaround times and costs, whilst operators benefit from higher capacity utilisation and lower per-mission overhead.

## Equity-Sharing: Betting on Onboard Success

Even a ‘space-compute’ model needs working capital. Borrowing biotech incubator mechanics, stations should offer reduced or waived access fees in exchange for:

*   **Royalties** on revenue generated by onboard products (for example, a share of drug sales)
    
*   **Equity Stakes** in startups that commercialise novel materials or technologies developed in microgravity
    

This approach turns an infrastructure cost center into an appreciating asset. Startups avoid prohibitive upfront fees, while station operators participate directly in the upside of every successful payload, aligning incentives for long-term collaboration and platform improvement.

# Building the Broader Orbital Ecosystem

With our two core business models in place, we must now cultivate the market and policy landscape that will sustain them. Commercial stations cannot succeed in isolation; they require a healthy, interdependent ecosystem.

## Creating Market Pull through Infrastructure

Station operators should become proactive market builders.

Emerging sectors such as in-space servicing, assembly and manufacturing and orbital logistics demand demonstration environments in orbit. By establishing dedicated robotics corridors, precision docking modules and standardised payload interfaces, stations can host regular technology validation campaigns in partnership with satellite operators and service providers. These testbeds reduce development risk for innovators and provide predictable cadence for station utilisation.

Long lead times and bespoke integration currently deter early adopters; a conveyor-belt approach to experiment integration, coupled with guaranteed uptime and on-station support services, will dramatically shorten sales cycles and lock in recurring revenues.

Beyond hardware, operators can curate thematic calls for proposals in areas such as refuelling robotics, modular habitat assembly and microgravity electronics fabrication. These campaigns, financed through modest user fees and sponsored by public-private consortia, will further stimulate demand and position the station as the proving ground of choice for next-generation orbital technologies.

## Global Co-Investment: From Users to Stakeholders

The next generation of stations must transform occasional customers into invested allies.

Rather than simply selling access, operators can structure co-investment vehicles that grant participating nations, agencies and commercial users an ownership stake in the station’s future. For example, a consortium of emerging spacefaring countries could contribute capital in return for equity shares proportionate to their investment. Similarly, anchor commercial customers, such as pharmaceutical companies or materials producers, could secure preferred rates in exchange for a minority equity stake or a capped royalty on their onboard revenues.

This model aligns long-term incentives and creates a stable capital base. Governance can be formalised through a station council composed of equity partners, ensuring strategic direction reflects stakeholder interests. By broadening the ownership roster beyond traditional partners, stations will benefit from diversified funding sources, enhanced diplomatic support and a ready-made customer pipeline. Passive users become part of the station’s board, deepening their commitment and reducing the risk of abrupt funding withdrawals.

Next-generation stations offer an opportunity to rebalance this model. India, Brazil, Saudi Arabia, South Korea, and the UAE are expanding their space sectors and have strategic, technical, and diplomatic incentives to participate. Co-investment, shared equity, and hosted national missions can turn passive interest into active partnership, broadening the financial base and enhancing geopolitical stability.

## Phasing Out Subsidies, Spurring Commercial Rev-Ops

Despite these new models, government funding remains essential for the near future.

Public funding remains essential during the station’s infancy, but it must be delivered in a way that encourages market maturity. A tiered subsidy framework offers a clear runway for commercial viability. In the first phase, governments cover 100 percent of pre-commercial research and development activities up to Technology Readiness Level 3, de-risking foundational experiments.

In the second phase, agencies transition to cost-sharing, funding 50 percent of integration and demonstration projects between TRL 4 and TRL 6. This model ensures that novel applications such as microgravity drug synthesis or precision manufacturing receive focused support without encouraging perpetual subsidy dependence. By TRL 7 and above, all operating costs shift to commercial users, who by then have validated revenue streams and repeat business models.

To facilitate this transition, agencies can offer milestone-based bridge contracts or revenue guarantees that taper as private orders increase. Clear sunset dates for each funding phase create urgency for commercial customers to prove their business cases.

This graduated approach not only incentivises private investment but also provides a predictable timeline for governments to exit operational funding, ensuring a sustainable handover from public subsidy to market-driven growth.

# A Roadmap Beyond the ISS: Your Next Steps

The end of the ISS era is not just a handover to the private sector. It is a chance to redefine what a space station is for. Without new thinking, commercial successors will inherit the same economic fragility.

Instead, we must adopt the platform-as-a-service and equity-sharing frameworks outlined above to create stations that generate value, attract users and compound returns over time.

To move from theory to reality, organisations should:

1.  **Pilot Modular Service Offerings**: Develop a small-scale demonstration of standardised modules and transparent pricing for microgravity experiments, using existing commercial vehicles or hosted payloads.
    
2.  **Structure Equity Partnerships**: Convene potential station customers, governments, commercial R&D firms and emerging space nations, to explore joint-investment agreements and royalty models that align long-term incentives.
    
3.  **Engage Policymakers**: Advocate for a tiered subsidy framework that supports low-TRL research, phases out operational grants by TRL 7 and introduces milestone-based bridge contracts.
    

By taking these steps now, stakeholders can ensure the next generation of space stations not only sustains itself but also expands what is possible in orbit, enabling new industries, partnerships and scientific breakthroughs.

But it must do more than sustain itself. It must create the conditions for what comes next. Commercial stations should not follow the ISS, they should make it possible to leave it behind.
