Beyond hardware, operators can curate thematic calls for proposals in areas such as refuelling robotics, modular habitat assembly and microgravity electronics fabrication. These campaigns, financed through modest user fees and sponsored by public-private consortia, will further stimulate demand and position the station as the proving ground of choice for next-generation orbital technologies.

Global Co-Investment: From Users to Stakeholders

The next generation of stations must transform occasional customers into invested allies.

Rather than simply selling access, operators can structure co-investment vehicles that grant participating nations, agencies and commercial users an ownership stake in the station’s future. For example, a consortium of emerging spacefaring countries could contribute capital in return for equity shares proportionate to their investment. Similarly, anchor commercial customers, such as pharmaceutical companies or materials producers, could secure preferred rates in exchange for a minority equity stake or a capped royalty on their onboard revenues.

This model aligns long-term incentives and creates a stable capital base. Governance can be formalised through a station council composed of equity partners, ensuring strategic direction reflects stakeholder interests. By broadening the ownership roster beyond traditional partners, stations will benefit from diversified funding sources, enhanced diplomatic support and a ready-made customer pipeline. Passive users become part of the station’s board, deepening their commitment and reducing the risk of abrupt funding withdrawals.

Next-generation stations offer an opportunity to rebalance this model. India, Brazil, Saudi Arabia, South Korea, and the UAE are expanding their space sectors and have strategic, technical, and diplomatic incentives to participate. Co-investment, shared equity, and hosted national missions can turn passive interest into active partnership, broadening the financial base and enhancing geopolitical stability.

Phasing Out Subsidies, Spurring Commercial Rev-Ops

Despite these new models, government funding remains essential for the near future.

Public funding remains essential during the station’s infancy, but it must be delivered in a way that encourages market maturity. A tiered subsidy framework offers a clear runway for commercial viability. In the first phase, governments cover 100 percent of pre-commercial research and development activities up to Technology Readiness Level 3, de-risking foundational experiments.

In the second phase, agencies transition to cost-sharing, funding 50 percent of integration and demonstration projects between TRL 4 and TRL 6. This model ensures that novel applications such as microgravity drug synthesis or precision manufacturing receive focused support without encouraging perpetual subsidy dependence. By TRL 7 and above, all operating costs shift to commercial users, who by then have validated revenue streams and repeat business models.

To facilitate this transition, agencies can offer milestone-based bridge contracts or revenue guarantees that taper as private orders increase. Clear sunset dates for each funding phase create urgency for commercial customers to prove their business cases.

This graduated approach not only incentivises private investment but also provides a predictable timeline for governments to exit operational funding, ensuring a sustainable handover from public subsidy to market-driven growth.

A Roadmap Beyond the ISS: Your Next Steps

The end of the ISS era is not just a handover to the private sector. It is a chance to redefine what a space station is for. Without new thinking, commercial successors will inherit the same economic fragility.

Instead, we must adopt the platform-as-a-service and equity-sharing frameworks outlined above to create stations that generate value, attract users and compound returns over time.

To move from theory to reality, organisations should:

  1. Pilot Modular Service Offerings: Develop a small-scale demonstration of standardised modules and transparent pricing for microgravity experiments, using existing commercial vehicles or hosted payloads.

  2. Structure Equity Partnerships: Convene potential station customers, governments, commercial R&D firms and emerging space nations, to explore joint-investment agreements and royalty models that align long-term incentives.

  3. Engage Policymakers: Advocate for a tiered subsidy framework that supports low-TRL research, phases out operational grants by TRL 7 and introduces milestone-based bridge contracts.

By taking these steps now, stakeholders can ensure the next generation of space stations not only sustains itself but also expands what is possible in orbit, enabling new industries, partnerships and scientific breakthroughs.

But it must do more than sustain itself. It must create the conditions for what comes next. Commercial stations should not follow the ISS, they should make it possible to leave it behind.

**Back to 1999: How space graduate pay has (not) changed**

Last year, at an ESA networking dinner in Spain, I spoke with a senior engineer who started his career in the British space sector in the late 1990s. His first graduate role paid over £20,000 a year, equivalent to about £45,000–£50,000 today once adjusted for inflation. Yet aerospace engineering graduates in the UK now typically start on £25,000–£35,000, with only a handful of roles breaching £40,000. In real terms, starting pay has barely budged in 25 years, despite soaring living costs, mounting student debt, and increasingly complex clearance requirements.

[

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/057699c3-c5e8-48da-b087-4af69208784a_902x472.png)



](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!z_gA!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F057699c3-c5e8-48da-b087-4af69208784a_902x472.png)

The salary for a British Space Engineering Graduate has fallen by 40% in real terms since 1999

It is not just a nominal stagnation, but a systemic undervaluing of technical talent. While minimum wage and cost-of-living pressures nudged headline salaries above £30,000, the underlying strategy remains one of underinvestment. If space is truly a strategic sector, it deserves strategic pay.

**Harwell: A Launchpad You Can't Afford**

Even the meagre salaries above are hollow if you cannot afford to live near the job.

Take Harwell. It’s promoted as the UK’s space innovation hub. It hosts the UK Space Agency, Open Cosmos, Satellite Applications Catapult, and numerous startups. On paper, it's a success, a walkable concentration of the nation’s top talent. In reality, it’s a car-dependent science park surrounded by Oxfordshire rents, with jobs that don’t even guarantee access to parking. I ran the numbers once to move to Harwell. I would have needed a £10,000 pay rise to match my lifestyle in Manchester, a location which is also expensive but somehow cheaper than Harwell.

At the time of writing, a room in a shared house near Harwell averages £834 per month. For a graduate on a £30,000 salary, post-tax take-home pay is around £1,970 per month. Rent alone takes up over 42% of their income, before bills, groceries, or transport.

This isn’t an edge case. It’s the default. Many of these “strategic” jobs are located in places where even shared housing is unaffordable on a graduate salary.

**The Unspoken Elite Track**

As Lindsay Clark noted in her original Register article, the space sector’s competitor for talent isn’t just banking and consulting; it’s every job that offers better pay and fewer barriers. Indeed, Clark cites entry-level salaries of **£80,000–£90,000** in investment banking and management consulting as eye-watering.

In reality, MBB roles start at £50k base, bulge-bracket banking analysts at £60k base, and HFTs like Jane Street at around £150k. But for the typical STEM graduate, these roles are effectively out of reach. Securing internships in your first year, navigating unpaid or low‑paid placements, and leveraging alumni networks at prestigious institutions form a gauntlet that excludes the majority.

I worked at a leading space consultancy and was one of the few without a Russell Group pedigree or a portfolio of internships. The rest came with the right CV, connections, and clearance, resources not available to most. The question is not whether UK space pay lags banking, it’s whether it competes with realistic alternatives.

**Beyond the UK: Europe Pays More**

Talent flows to where it is paid, and Europe is taking note.

I lived in mainland Europe for several years, both before and after Brexit. The shift is obvious. Before, the UK was a top destination for space talent, English-speaking, globally connected, and relatively well-paid. That appeal has declined dramatically.

I recently spent a month in Torino, home to several Italian space firms. Over aperitifs, I spoke with engineers at both startups and major primes. None said they would consider relocating to the UK… not because of weather, culture, or visa bureaucracy, but because they’d earn the same, or more, staying in Italy. With the post-Brexit slide in the pound and high UK living costs, the economics simply don’t work. I appreciate this is anecdotal evidence, so I have also grabbed some salary datapoints from across Europe.

**Italy**: Leonardo’s graduate engineers report starting salaries of **€33,000–€35,000** (£28,000–£30,000), with clear, incremental increases around year two and three. Combined with lower rents outside Milan and strong public healthcare, the real take-home is competitive with UK figures, if not better.

**Germany**: Under IG Metall agreements, entry roles begin at **€50,000–€65,000** (£42,000–£55,000), escalating by union-negotiated cost-of-living raises. Generous sick pay, 30 days leave, and robust unemployment benefits add to the package. Here, an engineer’s wage goes beyond salary to genuine livelihood security.

**Netherlands & Sweden**: Early-career roles in ESA-affiliated sites like Noordwijk pay **€45,000–€60,000** (£38,000–£50,000), sometimes with housing allowances and subsidised transport. In Stockholm or Gothenburg, space-adjacent tech jobs in satcom and sensor fusion fetch similar figures, alongside shorter working weeks and parental support

[

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/a6cf706f-a0df-47b3-8cbb-c41ea50f09e9_884x463.png)



](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!76fs!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa6cf706f-a0df-47b3-8cbb-c41ea50f09e9_884x463.png)

British graduate roles pay closer to Italian wages than German ones

**Introducing Dishoom, where pouring pints pays beats space engineering on pay**

If continental Europe outbids us, what about domestic competition? Shelter from austerity rarely comes from public coffers, but rather from the hospitality sector.

I gathered current data from Glassdoor, Gradcracker, and company career pages:

*   **Graduate space roles**: £28,000–£34,000
    
*   **Specialist positions**: up to £40,000
    
*   **Senior 5‑year engineers**: £35,000–£45,000
    

By contrast, at Dishoom, a well‑run, tip‑inclusive restaurant group, servers earn:

*   **£16/hr base** = £33,280/year
    
*   **£18–20/hr with tips** = £37,000–£41,000/year
    
*   **Team Management** \= up to £45,000
    

[

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/6f67c701-048a-4581-a417-5984c2b981f2_830x434.png)



](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4rAd!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6f67c701-048a-4581-a417-5984c2b981f2_830x434.png)

Space engineering is a strategically important industry, but you’d get paid the same serving curries

No degree, no clearance, no multi-stage hiring. Just consistent, fair pay. In effect, a server at Dishoom can out‑earn an engineer designing satellite subsystems, especially when you realise they don’t face student loan payments.

This isn’t a criticism of hospitality, far from it. It’s refreshing to see a company pay staff properly. The issue is the disconnect between how we talk about ‘strategic sectors’ like space, and how we actually treat the people expected to work in them. If the UK wants to build a sovereign capability, it cannot rely on goodwill and underpaid engineers.

[

![](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/448a0315-077f-4459-8295-da2ba10517df_899x471.png)



](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ptbY!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F448a0315-077f-4459-8295-da2ba10517df_899x471.png)

British engineering salaries not only cannot compete with Europe, but you’d be better off serving curries than building satellites

**Space Sovereignty Starts with a Competitive Paycheck**

We champion STEM education, publish space strategy white papers, and promise sovereignty in orbit. But sovereignty requires people.

Right now, the UK space sector offers:

*   **Starting salaries** that have fallen behind inflation and continental peers
    
*   **Locations** that exclude the very graduates we need
    
*   **Progression** that lags service and software industr
    

The result is a brain drain not to Wall Street, but to hospitality, European labs, and tech hubs that value engineers properly.

Here’s the unsparing truth:

**You can earn more serving curries than building satellites.**

Until government and industry align pay with promise, the UK will continue to lose its brightest, and space will remain a distant dream rather than a national achievement.

Not to Silicon Valley. Not to Wall Street. Just to somewhere they can pay their rent.

As you are reading this, tens of thousands of satellites are streaking overhead. They are monitoring our crops, guiding our cars, and beaming calls from the most remote corners of the globe. But, as their numbers swell, a looming threat remains overhead. If even a 1cm spec of debris collides with a spacecraft, it can make the million dollar machine inoperable. Worse than that, if the collision is severe enough, there is a risk that the impacted satellite might shatter into thousands of additional pieces of debris, each of which could collide with further satellites in a runaway loop that could render space unusable for generations.

# The relationship between satellites in orbit and collision avoidance

This is a known issue within the industry, but I am writing it today after reading [Hugh Lewis](https://www.linkedin.com/in/hugh-lewis-31242117/)’ [analysis of Starlink’s latest semi-annual report.](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/starlink-manoeuvre-update-july-2025-hugh-lewis-utkhe/?trackingId=N87tkJD8esU01XWVzjUgEw%3D%3D) This analysis outlined that 144,000 avoidance burns were executed within six months, nearly double the previous rate. Lewis’ analysis reveal an alarming trend: as Starlink’s population climbs, the yearly collision-avoidance manoeuvre rate explodes. Figure 1, taken from the analysis, plots the annual burns against the average number of active satellites, fitting an exponential curve.

[

![A graph showing the annual manoeuvre rate as a function of the average number of working satellites. The trendline is exponential with R^2 = 0.9772.](https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/9dbdddfa-a4db-4c6f-8edc-c1a0fdcc2f19_1259x823.png "A graph showing the annual manoeuvre rate as a function of the average number of working satellites. The trendline is exponential with R^2 = 0.9772.")



](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!up66!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9dbdddfa-a4db-4c6f-8edc-c1a0fdcc2f19_1259x823.png)

Annual manoeuvre rate as a function of the average number of working Starlink satellites. The gradient of this trendline provides an estimate of the manoeuvre rate per satellite per year. \[Source: Lewis, H. “Starlink Manoeuvre Update July 2025,” LinkedIn (2 July 2025)\]

It’s a harsh signal that our ground-based, human-in-the-loop processes are rapidly hitting their limits. Even accounting for Starlink tightening it’s probability threshold, this curve shows that each additional thousand satellites adds disproportionately more burns, rapidly overwhelming ground-based operations.

# Starlink can act as a proxy for the industry as a whole

You might be wondering, “Why just Starlink?”. Well, they’re the biggest operator who issues semi-annual reports that provide a rare, consistent multi-year insight into how avoidance burns stack up as satellites multiply. Most other operators do no put this level of detail into the open, so Starlink’s numbers are our best proxy for the true operational burden we face up here.

As satellite fleets and debris clouds multiply, our current collision-avoidance methods will buckle under the load. Relying on ground stations and human-in-the-loop decisions introduces delays, uncertainty, and cost at every turn. Here are the biggest headaches we face today:

1.  **Latency in Detection and Response**
    
2.  **Ballooning Alert Volumes**
    
3.  **Rapidly Growing Uncertainty**
    
4.  **Fragmented Tracking Data**
    
5.  **Coordination Overhead**
    
6.  **Fuel and Lifetime Trade-Offs**
    
7.  **High Relative Velocities**
    

To think in more general terms, if the problem you’re trying to solve is growing exponentially, any solution that scales linearly, or worse, relies on humans, will quickly collapse under its own weight. We need a collision-avoidance method that scales at least as fast as the threat: one that pushes sensing, decision-making, and maneuver execution onboard each spacecraft, rather than shuttling data back and forth to Earth. This shift from ground-centric to distributed, autonomous operations is the only way to keep pace with the coming tidal wave of satellites and debris. Whether this is a literal movement of computing onto the satellites themselves, onto data centres in orbit, or even done autonomously on a satellite-by-satellite basis is up to better minds than myself.

# This is a problem we’ve solved before

At first glance, this sounds like a really hard problem, right? Imagine trying to track tens of thousands of satellites, each zooming along at thousands of miles an hour, against a backdrop of millions of debris fragments, and doing it all without a single centralized beacon or traffic controller. Yet every day, some 12,000–14,000 aircraft crisscross our skies with near-perfect safety records, despite being built by different manufacturers, flown by crews speaking different languages, and guided by many different air-traffic systems.

How do the planes not crash into each other? The secret is an on-board, peer-to-peer system fitted onto nearly every commercial plane. This system continuously sends and listens for specific radio signals from nearby aircraft. By timing how long these signals take to return, the system can build a live, 3D map of surrounding traffic. If another plane gets too close, it’ll warn the pilot, and if the pilot doesn’t resolve it, it will issue a message to tell the pilot of one plane to climb and the other plane to descend, without the need for ground control to be involved, using a computer, an antenna, and a cockpit display.

As someone with an interest in air crash investigation, it’s well known that early planes were much more dangerous. The need for a TCAS-like system was first seen in the mid-20th century after the 1956 Grand Canyon mid-air collision when two perfect condition passenger aircraft crashed into each other, resulting in the creation of the FAA.

In the following decades, further collisions revealed that “see‑and‑avoid” procedures and intermittent radar coverage were inadequate. Investigations repeatedly found that neither pilots nor controllers had reliable, real‑time awareness of nearby traffic. # **So why does space not have TCAS**

Even though orbit is becoming as congested as our skies, a TCAS‑style solution for satellites runs into three major roadblocks:

1.  **No universal beacon**. Satellites rely on a patchwork of ground radar stations, optical telescopes and proprietary links, each with its own quirks of accuracy, delay and access. Without a common “space transponder”, they simply cannot share real-time positions.
    
2.  **Harsh orbital conditions**. Debris and satellites whip by at over 10 km/s, and safe manoeuvres must be planned hours or even days ahead. Fitting the precise sensors and computing power needed to predict these encounters into every small LEO craft strains weight, power and thermal limits.
    
3.  **Fragmented rule making**. Aviation had ICAO and the FAA to hammer out global standards; in space, dozens of national agencies, military bodies and commercial operators each guard their own orbit data and procedures. Agreeing on a single protocol and trusting autonomous systems to fire thrusters without human sign‑off will take time, co‑ordination and probably a few more close calls.
    

# But I think it is possible

However, nearly every satellite already carries a basic telecommand-and-telemetry antenna. By piggy‑backing a lightweight beacon onto that existing link, sending only position and status, neighbouring spacecraft could listen in and plan avoidance. They would pick up each other’s beacons, build a live, peer-to-peer traffic map and decide onboard whether to manoeuvre.

Modern satellites now pack surprisingly powerful, energy‑efficient computers and tiny radar or laser sensors into a small package, all drawing only a small amount of power. By ramping up computing only when needed and using simple passive cooling, these components can run real‑time calculations and spot objects under a metre away without adding significant weight or complexity. As a result, even the smallest satellites can support an onboard system that detects nearby craft or debris and makes manoeuvre decisions autonomously.

Another issue is that space, unlike airspace, is not owned or controlled by any single nation, so there is no ICAO‑style authority to mandate a common beacon. Yet almost every major satellite programme depends in some way on US or EU government funding, licences or launch services. By making the carriage of a standard “Space Traffic Transponder” a condition of export approvals, launch contracts or grant awards, much as the FAA tied Mode C/S transponders to aircraft certification, regulators could force universal adoption. Over time, this approach would copy aviation’s top‑down mandate in orbit, even without a single global space authority.

The final challenge is standardisation. Despite the many ‘standards’ in the industry, if you ever speak with a RF engineer they’ll tell you it’s more myth than reality. I naively assumed that something like ‘CCSDS compliant’ would mean they followed the standards, but a much smarter RF engineer than me explained that even the manufacturer’s data sheets contradict themselves and it’s much harder to be compatible than it seems.

**A Grave Warning for Orbit**

In aviation, regulations were written in blood, shaped by the sacrifices of pilots and passengers who died before systems like TCAS became mandatory. In space, without people aboard to galvanise action, catastrophic debris cascades won’t command the same urgency. If we do not adopt that hard‑won, life‑or‑death mindset and make onboard collision avoidance a compulsory standard, we risk condemning the orbital commons to an environmental crisis from which it may never recover.

As you are reading this, tens of thousands of satellites are streaking overhead. They are monitoring our crops, guiding our cars, and beaming calls from the most remote corners of the globe. Worse than that, if the collision is severe enough, there is a risk that the impacted satellite might shatter into thousands of additional pieces of debris, each of which could collide with further satellites in a runaway loop that could render space unusable for generations.

# **The structural habit of doing the right thing**

As anyone who has met me knows, I am always travelling somewhere. However, there’s one place I’ve consistently returned to. Hamburg, a bustling port city in northern Germany which has many parallels with my home city of Manchester. From the red brick buildings by the canals, to the underground music scene, and even to the uprising of overpriced, venture capital backed coffee shops.

Despite the vast array of similarities, there is one major difference that always sticks with me whenever I return to the UK. The idea of civic responsibility that sits deep within the German mindset. It is the small things that impress me, where Germans regularly take actions for the greater good of society. This includes things like the infamous quiet hours, where you cannot so much as turn on a washing machine too late at night without risking disturbing the peace. This stretches further: within the first few weeks of living in Germany several years ago I was publicly and sharply criticised by strangers, often grandmas, for crossing the road before the light went green, and even now I am impressed by the fact that German parks often have dedicated BBQ sections which are filled with hundreds of people, including immigrants and other foreigners, who are meticulously following the rules.

This civic responsibility isn’t innate to Germans; it is engineered by public policy. As the title suggests, the part that impresses me most is the Pfand system: a deposit return scheme where every drink container carries a small, refundable stake. You pay it at purchase and get it back when you return the empty bottle or can, drop it in a reverse vending machine or hand it to the shop, and the system does the rest. The deposit is large enough that people care, small enough not to feel punitive, and the logistics are frictionless, so compliance becomes the default; return rates sit around 98 percent.

Crucially, it internalises the cost of waste without preaching: if you don’t return the container, you lose the deposit, which in aggregate funds the system’s operation and creates a buffer for sustainability, while responsible behaviour is rewarded immediately. That is the logic I want to transplant to orbit, a refundable “orbital Pfand” posted up front, returned only after verified end of life disposal or safe deorbiting, with forfeited stakes underwriting cleanup or compensating future users.

# **Why Sustainability Fails Today**

Yes, I can hear the obvious objection, I run a space consulting firm, why invoke German civic society? Because the mechanism that makes compliance habitual in Hamburg is the same structural lever missing in orbital governance. As the NewSpace industry is rapidly maturing, I believe that the system should be built in a responsible way, one that looks after the shared commons of low Earth orbit. At the moment, there are countless efforts led by well-meaning groups to improve space sustainability. Almost every major space agency trots out sustainability as a headline, with new research being funded every year. A specific example of this is the European Space Agency’s Zero Debris Charter, a non-legally binding initiative that is fostering a community of proactive actors working collectively towards jointly defined, measurable targets for 2030.

The language can feel dense and bureaucratic, but there are specific and quantitative goals inside, including avoiding intentional debris release and keeping the probability of space debris generation below one in a thousand over an object’s lifetime. Fine, on paper. But this, alongside almost all other standards, are voluntary agreements with no binding teeth. We are currently relying on commercial actors whose fiduciary obligations push them to maximise shareholder returns to voluntarily constrain behaviour that degrades a shared commons over time.

Once again, as I always say, this is not a new problem unique to the space industry. It is a concept as old as classical economic thought, more commonly known as the tragedy of the commons. This is where, if many people enjoy unrestricted access to a finite, valuable resource, most typically referring to a pasture, they will tend to overuse it and it often ends up with the destruction of the shared good. The term was popularised by Garrett Hardin in his 1968 article titled “The Tragedy of the Commons,” although its roots trace back to William Forster Lloyd’s earlier pamphlet, Two Lectures on the Checks to Population, which used the example of cattle herders sharing common grazing land. Lloyd noted that the individually rational decision would be for each farmer to add more cattle, but if every farmer did that, the pasture would be depleted.

Therein is the tragedy.

“Each man is locked into a system that compels him to increase his herd without limit, in a world that is limited. Ruin is the destination toward which all men rush, each pursuing his own best interest in a society that believes in the freedom of the commons. Freedom in a commons brings ruin to all.”  
– Garrett Hardin, _The Tragedy of the Commons_, _Science_, 1968

# **The Structural Fault Lines in the Space Economy**

This is especially problematic given the economic system we find ourselves in. The vast majority of satellites today are operated by companies, either publicly traded or, more commonly, backed by private investors who are, rightly, seeking to maximise the return on their investments. Every modern company is racing to launch more satellites, serve more customers, and increase the return to shareholders. The misalignment in the space industry is amplified by four structural factors:

*   Humans are poor at accurately estimating risks, they systematically underestimate tail risk because conventional risk models assume thin tails and rely on misleading averages. Catastrophes like the 2008 financial crisis, COVID-19 and climate change exposed these failures. Even professional risk managers mispriced the likelihood and consequences. Taleb’s _[Statistical Consequences of Fat Tails](https://codowd.com/bigdata/misc/Taleb_Statistical_Consequences_of_Fat_Tails.pdf)_ is a rigorous, if lengthy, treatment of this.
    
*   The actors creating space debris are not the ones who will bear its full cost. Immediate economic gains from launching and operating additional satellites accrue privately, while the cumulative degradation of the orbital environment, higher collision probabilities, reduced access, cascade risks, is felt collectively by future users. That creates a classic negative externality with perverse incentive alignment.
    
*   Commercial actors are structurally short termist. Investors and markets reward rapid deployment and revenue growth, so companies prioritise near term returns over preserving orbital sustainability. You might think you are an ethical space engineer, but there is a strong chance your space startup will be acquired by private equity firms and its original values diluted or discarded.
    
*   No one owns orbit, so individual choices add up to collective harm. Each operator acting in their own interest increases traffic and systemic risk, collisions generate debris, which further destabilises the environment in feedback loops. There is no global enforcement authority, no space environmental protection agency, no effective adjudication mechanism.
    

# **For a sustainable future in space**

Space sustainability isn’t a technical problem waiting for a better model, it is an incentive problem. The Pfand shows the fix: require operators to post a refundable, risk calibrated stake, return it only after independently verified end of life behaviour, and use forfeited deposits to fund cleanup or compensate future users. Embed that mechanism in licences, financing covenants and procurement. Launch pilots with a coalition of willing states and commercial partners, and publish performance publicly. Give actors skin in the game, and the race to overload orbit becomes a mechanism for its stewardship, fail to do so and humanity may be stuck on Earth looking up at an impassable field of debris caused by our actions today.

The recent announcement that the **[UK Space Agency](https://www.linkedin.com/company/uk-space-agency/)** will be absorbed into its parent department, the **[Department for Science, Innovation and Technology](https://www.linkedin.com/company/scitechgovuk/)**, has triggered headlines suggesting the end of Britain’s space ambitions. That is overstated. The change is real, but it is primarily a restructuring, UKSA will lose its status as an executive agency and instead become a directorate within DSIT. Its programmes and teams will continue, but its independence, visibility, and ability to speak with authority will be diminished.

To understand the implications, it helps to step back and look at how the UK government is organised. Space policy sits within a complex Whitehall system of departments, agencies, and regulators, each with distinct responsibilities. Misreporting often comes from treating all of these as “the government” without recognising the hierarchy or the difference between setting policy and delivering programmes.

A brief explainer of what is changing, as you can see, this is a relatively minor change, with the space ecosystem still being spread out

## **To begin, what is meant by the government in the UK?**

In the UK, the general public has the tendency to call everything from the police to the Prime Minister ‘the government’. This is strictly speaking incorrect, and when discussing government body restructuring, it is important to understand exactly what is being talked about.

The government is the executive branch of the state, similar in role to the President of the United States and their Cabinet. It is the body responsible for running the country, developing policy, and drafting laws. Today, this is led by Sir Keir Starmer, the Prime Minister, who has appointed 29 Cabinet Ministers to his government.

Not every minister heads a department. Some Cabinet Ministers do, for example, the Secretary of State for Defence runs the Ministry of Defence. Others hold cross-cutting or portfolio roles without their own department, such as the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, who sits in the Cabinet Office to coordinate government policy, or the Minister without Portfolio, who focuses on political and party matters.

For space, this top layer matters because it decides whether space is treated as a strategic national priority. The Cabinet Office plays a central role here. It supports the Prime Minister, ensures policy is joined up across Whitehall, and manages the system of Cabinet Committees that make decisions on specific issues.

One such committee was the National Space Council, created in 2020 to coordinate the UK’s civil and defence space policy. Chaired at Cabinet level and supported by the **[Cabinet Office](https://www.linkedin.com/company/cabinet-office/)**, its purpose was to align the work of departments such as DSIT, **[Department for Business and Trade](https://www.linkedin.com/company/department-for-business-and-trade/)**, and the **[FCDO Services](https://www.linkedin.com/company/fcdo-services/)** under a unified space strategy. Although it is now largely dormant, its creation demonstrated that space was considered important enough to require attention at the highest political level, on par with national security and economic policy.

## **Ministerial Departments**

Beneath the Prime Minister and Cabinet sit the ministerial departments. These are the core Whitehall organisations that turn political direction into policy and manage the government machine. Each is led by a Secretary of State and staffed by politically neutral civil servants.

For space, six departments matter:

*   **Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT)**: the lead civil space department. It contains the Space Directorate, the policy unit responsible for setting national space strategy. DSIT also houses the Geospatial Commission, which coordinates the use of geospatial data across government.
    
*   **Ministry of Defence (MoD)**: home to the Defence Space Directorate, which shapes military space policy and ensures it is integrated into wider national defence and security planning.
    
*   **Department for Transport (DfT)**: its Aviation, Maritime and Security Group covers spaceflight policy, including the framework for launches and spaceports.
    
*   **Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO)**: contains a Space and Advanced Technologies team, which leads UK engagement in space diplomacy, international treaties, and forums such as the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space.
    
*   **Department for Business and Trade (DBT)**: maintains policy teams dedicated to trade and investment in the space sector, promoting UK capabilities abroad and encouraging inward investment.
    
*   **HM Treasury**: does not have a dedicated space unit, but its spending and infrastructure teams control the flow of funding into space, from European Space Agency subscriptions to national satellite projects.
    

Together, these departments and their internal policy units form the policy backbone for UK space. They decide strategy, coordinate across government, and determine the financial framework that underpins delivery.

## **Executive Agencies: the delivery arms of departments**

Departments set policy, but they do not always deliver programmes themselves. Instead, they often rely on executive agencies, specialist units that are part of the civil service but operate at arm’s length. Each has a chief executive who runs the organisation, while a minister remains accountable to Parliament for its performance.

For space, the key executive agencies are:

*   **UK Space Agency (DSIT)**: the government’s civil space delivery arm. It turns national space strategy into practice, manages the UK’s contributions to international programmes such as the European Space Agency, and runs national funding schemes for science and industry.
    
*   **Met Office (DSIT)**: best known for weather forecasts, but also a crucial provider of space weather services. It monitors solar storms and provides warnings that protect satellites, power grids, and aviation systems.
    
*   **Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (Dstl, MoD)**: the MoD’s in-house research agency. While it covers the full range of defence science, it has a significant space element, including work on sensors, secure communications, and counter-space resilience.
    

These agencies show how government policy moves from Whitehall strategies into real-world activity: funding missions, providing warnings, and developing technologies. They are the bridge between departments and the frontline of delivery.

## **Executive NDPBs: independent regulators and funders**

Executive agencies sit inside the civil service, but some functions are considered too sensitive or too specialised to be run directly by ministers. In these cases, government creates Executive Non-Departmental Public Bodies (NDPBs). These are legally separate organisations, with their own boards and chief executives. Ministers set the policy framework and provide funding, but cannot interfere in their day-to-day decisions.

For space, the most important Executive NDPBs are:

*   **Civil Aviation Authority (CAA, DfT)**: the UK’s independent aviation and spaceflight regulator. Since 2021, the CAA has been responsible for issuing launch licences, overseeing spaceports, and regulating orbital operations under the Space Industry Act.
    
*   **UK Research and Innovation (DSIT)**: the UK’s main research funding body. It supports space science and technology through its research councils, including the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC) and Innovate UK, which focus on major facilities, research funding, and industry innovation.
    
*   **Satellite Applications Catapult (via Innovate UK, within UKRI, under DSIT)** – part of a network of “Catapults” created to accelerate innovation. It helps businesses and researchers turn satellite data into commercial services, from agriculture to telecommunications.
    

These organisations illustrate a different model of governance. While still funded by government, they are designed to make decisions independently, whether that means regulating launch safety, awarding research grants, or supporting commercialisation.

## **Public Corporations: government-owned but commercial**

Some government bodies are expected to operate much more like companies. These are called Public Corporations. They are government-owned, but unlike agencies or NDPBs they generate most of their income from commercial sales rather than direct grant funding. They still serve a public role, but their business model is closer to the private sector.

In the space and geospatial field, the main example is:

*   **Ordnance Survey (OS, DSIT)**: the UK’s national mapping agency. While it has a public duty to maintain accurate national maps, most of its income comes from selling geospatial data and digital services. OS makes heavy use of satellite imagery and Earth observation data in its work, making it directly relevant to the wider space sector.
    

Public Corporations like OS show a different side of government involvement: they are publicly owned but commercially driven, sitting at the intersection of the state and the market.

## **Quangos, ALBs, and the jargon**

The term quango (quasi-autonomous non-governmental organisation) is old political slang for bodies that are government-funded but operate at arm’s length. It isn’t an official category.

Today the proper term is Arm’s-Length Body (ALB). This is the umbrella for:

*   **Executive Agencies** (inside the civil service, semi-autonomous),
    
*   **Executive NDPBs** (independent legal bodies with boards), and
    
*   **Public Corporations** (government-owned but commercial).
    

In short: every “quango” is an ALB, but not every ALB looks the same.

## **So what is happening to the UK Space Agency?**

The UK Space Agency is currently an Executive Agency of DSIT, which means it sits inside the civil service, with a chief executive, its own identity, but formally part of the department. The government has now announced that, as part of a cost-cutting and streamlining exercise, the Agency will be folded directly into DSIT. In practice, this means it will cease to be an Executive Agency and instead become a policy and delivery unit within the department itself.

## **Should you be worried?**

The announcement has generated alarmist headlines, but the reality is more mixed. The most important point is that the UK Space Agency’s core functions do not disappear. It will still manage Britain’s subscriptions to the European Space Agency, oversee national funding schemes, and coordinate civil space policy. The same teams will continue their work, only now as part of DSIT rather than as a stand-alone agency.

What does change is the status of the organisation. The Agency will lose its position as a separate executive agency, along with its chief executive, and instead become a directorate inside the department. That means it will no longer speak with the same institutional identity as bodies such as the Met Office or DVLA, but rather as one of several units inside DSIT. Its visibility and brand will inevitably be weaker, and it will have less day-to-day autonomy when it comes to technical or programmatic decisions.

We've actually already seen similar changes before, a few years back the former science department, BEIS, decide to revoke the UK Space Agency's space policy responsibilities and instead leave it more of a delivery agency. Although perhaps a more apt example is the Geospatial Commission. When it was created in 2018, it sat in the Cabinet Office with its own commissioners, a dedicated secretariat, and a high profile across government. Its job was to set national geospatial strategy and coordinate the “Geo6” bodies such as Ordnance Survey and the UK Hydrographic Office. Over time, however, that independence was eroded. First it was treated more like a standard policy unit within the Cabinet Office, and later it was absorbed into the Government Digital Service and now into DSIT. What began as a semi-autonomous, flagship initiative is today just another directorate inside a department, a trajectory the UK Space Agency now appears to be following.

The risk is that space becomes a lower priority, competing for political attention alongside DSIT’s wider responsibilities for digital policy, AI, and technology regulation. Internationally, the UK may look less prominent compared to countries with strong, independent agencies like CNES in France or DLR in Germany.

Yet there is also an upside: folding the Agency into DSIT may reduce administrative costs and bring space policy closer to the heart of government’s wider science and technology strategy, which has been a stated ambition for several years.

One potential benefit of folding the Space Agency into DSIT is a reduction in duplication. At present, space policy and funding roles are scattered across a patchwork of organisations: the Agency itself, DSIT’s Space Directorate, UKRI, STFC, and the Satellite Applications Catapult all recruit people to do strikingly similar work.

From my own experience applying to positions across these bodies, I have seen near-identical job descriptions repeated under different banners. Consolidation could streamline this system, cut administrative overhead, and make responsibilities clearer, though whether that efficiency gain outweighs the loss of visibility remains to be seen.

## **What does everyone else do?**

Most major space powers maintain strong, independent agencies, NASA in the US, CNES in France and DLR in Germany all operate with their own leadership, budgets and brand identity, giving them political weight at home and credibility abroad. By contrast, the UK’s plan to fold the Space Agency into DSIT aligns it more with countries such as Australia and New Zealand, where “space agencies” function as departmental units rather than stand-alone bodies. This approach is not unique, but it places Britain closer to mid-tier models that prioritise administrative efficiency over visibility, rather than the big-agency structures that dominate international space cooperation.

## **Conclusion**

In short, this is not the abolition of UKSA. “The UK will still have a civil space programme. But with the Space Agency folded into Whitehall machinery, Britain risks being seen less as a space power in its own right and more as a mid-tier player managing space alongside digital policy and AI. Whether that trade-off is worth it will only become clear over time.

When most people think about space, the same images come to mind: astronauts aboard the International Space Station, or the latest dramatic launch of a new rocket. These are spectacular moments that capture the imagination, but they are not where most of the real economic or societal value of space lies. Satellites orbiting above us already underpin the systems we rely on every day, whether we realise it or not. One of the least appreciated but most important areas where this impact is felt is in energy.

Working in the space sector, I often find myself having to explain to friends, family, and even taxi drivers why space matters. The conversation usually goes through the same predictable beats: no, I do not work for NASA, and no, I am not employed by SpaceX. When pressed further, I tend to rely on obvious examples of public good. It is easy enough to explain that satellites carry advanced cameras that can detect forest fires as they start, or monitor droughts from orbit, or measure crop moisture to help farmers increase yields. These examples are tangible, and they resonate with the average person.

Yet focusing too heavily on them risks missing out on other domains that are just as critical, and perhaps even more so in the years ahead. Among these overlooked areas, energy may well be the one where space makes the biggest difference in the coming decade. This article exists to explain a few novel applications in the energy field to make your taxi rides a little bit more varied.

## **What do we mean by energy**

When we talk about energy, we are not speaking in abstract terms about a far-off policy goal. Energy is the lifeblood of the modern economy and one of Europe’s greatest vulnerabilities. The Russian invasion of Ukraine made this clear. Europe’s dependence on Russian gas left governments scrambling to secure new supplies, prop up prices for consumers, and prevent entire industries from collapsing. At the same time, China’s dominance in solar manufacturing and critical minerals has reshaped global dependencies, creating new risks and limiting Europe’s room for manoeuvre. Energy has become as much a matter of geopolitics and national security as of engineering.

The scale is staggering. The European Union spends hundreds of billions of euros each year on energy imports. Meanwhile, policymakers are attempting to decarbonise grids, integrate massive amounts of renewable energy, electrify transport, and build hydrogen infrastructure. Every stage of this system carries enormous cost and complexity.

One way to break it down is into four broad phases of the energy lifecycle: generation, storage and distribution, operations and maintenance, and decommissioning and recycling.

1.  Generation covers the production of power through renewables, fossil fuels, or nuclear.
    
2.  Storage and distribution involves pipelines, grids, and increasingly hydrogen networks.
    
3.  Operations and maintenance means the day-to-day work of keeping the lights on, ensuring reliability, and cutting costs.
    
4.  Decommissioning and recycling concerns the safe retirement of ageing assets and the reduction of environmental impact from old infrastructure.
    

Each of these stages is vast, politically sensitive, and economically critical. Importantly, each also offers opportunities where space data can reduce costs, increase resilience, or improve environmental performance. That is what makes energy such a compelling case for space applications: it is not about speculative benefits in the distant future, but about tangible benefits that would bring down your energy bills.

## **What Is Space for Energy?**

Sure, energy is important. But, what does it have to do with space? The answer is not science fiction. Satellites already provide tools that deliver value to energy companies today, across the full lifecycle of energy, today.

### **Generation: Hydropower Forecasting via Satellite**

Firstly, hydropower remains the backbone of Europe’s renewable energy mix, with more than 100 gigawatts of installed capacity spread across Europe. Yet, hydro is uniquely vulnerable to something as simple as seasoning swings in rain and snowfall. We’re dealing with this today in the UK, with record low reservoirs in a dry summer. Operators, without careful forecasting, either have too much water in the reservoirs which wastes water and money, or they leave them too empty during summer, forcing them to buy electricity at a higher cost. Either way, that’s tens of millions of pounds wasted per reservoir.

This is where space comes in. Take SnowPower, a recent EOMAP-led ESA project which has been running since winter 2024 which delivers data on snow using novel remote sensing techniques to provide information on snow depth and snow water equivalent using Europe’s Sentinel-1 SAR satellites. This data allows users to know how much water is stored as snow in the catchment area, at a much lower cost than sending a guy with a sensor round to check it.

### **Storage and Distribution: Methane Leak Detection and Pipeline Monitoring**

Another key point to mention is methane, a short-lived gas that traps 84x more heat than carbon dioxide over a 20-year period and has resulted in 30% of today’s global warming. This gets worse when you consider that the **[International Energy Agency estimates that the production and use of fossil fuels results in close to 120 million tonnes of methane emissions in 2023, with 5Mt of methane from major fossil fuel leaks around the world](https://www.iea.org/reports/global-methane-tracker-2024/key-findings)**. However, to but my business perspective on. This is not just about global warming, rather every single gram of methane emitted is a gram of methane not sold for profit and the leaks cause untold financial penalties in the form of fines.

Enter Methane Watch, an ESA-funded project by Kayrros SAS, which detects large-scale methane emissions using the Sentinel, Landsat, and other satellites. Satellites are especially important in this area as methane is very technically challenging to measure as it leaks across the whole energy supply chain over time. Without frequent, cross border sensing, these emissions are basically unseen and impossible to fix.

This gets even worse for the operators once we consider regulations. Organisation such as the EU are launching new strategies that mandate leak detection with fines for non-compliance. In the face of this, satellite imagery is perhaps the most important tool to enforce these regulations, with new and improves satellites launching every year to improve monitoring capabilities.

### **Operation and Maintenance: Vegetation Encroachment**

The next stage in the energy lifecycle is operation and maintenance. This could be a puzzling part of the chain to include, as obviously satellites cannot operate powerplants. Yet, you just need to think wider, about all operational costs.

Take the US for example. There are millions of trees right next to the National Grid’s electricity assets. The grid spends hundreds of millions of dollars per year on maintaining and mitigating risks to the infrastructure because of this. As the climate changes, storms and more frequent, and this represents a risk to your electricity supply as just one tree could cut it off. Traditionally, as per the other applications, this was investigated by sending out staff, drones, or helicopters, all of which work on a small scale but cannot scale without cost.

To solve this, companies such as AiDASH uses satellite data to allow organisations to manage tree growth near transmission and distribution lines. When this is combined with new techniques related to AI, tree management systems are able to predict growth many years in advance, allowing for trims, removals and herbicides to be deployed to save the power grid.

In a Massachusetts pilot, **[AiDASH allowed the National Grid to optimise the scheduling of vegetation pruning from 5 years to 6 years](https://www.aidash.com/resource/aidash-transforming-vegetation-management-for-national-grid-using-satellite-analytics-and-ai/)** , as well as highlighting hotspots of risk for tree falling. You might think that a mere 1 year increase in the time between pruning is not a lot, but in reality, that is a saving of 17% in terms of cost and manhours.

### **End of Life: Decommissioning Offshore Oil and Gas Platforms**

The final stage of the energy lifecycle is decommissioning, retiring oil platforms, offshore wind farms, nuclear plants, or coal assets. On the surface, it sounds straightforward: lock up and throw away the key. But in reality, it’s one of the most complex, expensive, and risk-laden stages. Decommissioning the 500+ offshore oil and gas platforms in the North Sea alone is expected to cost over €50 billion by 2040.

Introducing new technology into this environment requires not only technical proof, but long cycles of validation, certification, and regulatory acceptance. For comparison, utilities typically evaluate grid upgrades on investment horizons of 20 to 40 years, far longer than the five-to-ten-year commercial timelines of most satellite service providers. That mismatch slows adoption to a crawl.

A second challenge is **procurement complexity**. Utilities are often semi-state bodies or regulated monopolies, with procurement processes designed to minimise perceived risk rather than maximise innovation. Tenders for vegetation management, for example, may be structured around helicopter patrol hours rather than outcomes like outages avoided. Even when satellite solutions are technically superior, they can struggle to fit into existing procurement frameworks. In Europe, some tenders run on cycles of three to five years, with renewal terms that lock incumbents in place and leave little room for new entrants.

A third factor is **legacy IT integration**. Utilities have invested billions in existing systems, grid management software, and asset databases over decades. These platforms are often proprietary, poorly documented, and resistant to integration. A satellite service that delivers imagery or alerts is of little value unless it can plug seamlessly into these existing workflows. Building that middleware layer is usually more expensive and time-consuming than acquiring the satellite data itself.

Each of these pressures creates opportunities for space-enabled monitoring, but also raises the bar for evidence. The best bargain in space may be about to go up in smoke, for no real reason. President Trump’s FY2026 budget moves to shut down two fully operational carbon monitoring satellites that remain the most precise instruments of their kind. These satellites have been built, paid for, and are still generating critical data, yet they are slated for termination to save a mere few million dollars a year. Europe should step in and secure them.

### **America Walks Away**

The Trump administration’s FY2026 budget proposal is blunt: OCO-2 and OCO-3 are to be switched off. NASA has been instructed to prepare decommissioning plans. For OCO-2, that means lowering its orbit until it burns up in the atmosphere; for OCO-3, simply powering down the instrument on the ISS. The justification is cost, but the numbers do not stand up to scrutiny. Annual operations are in the low tens of millions of dollars, barely noticeable within NASA’s budget and negligible compared to the billions already invested in Earth observation.

This is not a decision driven by technical obsolescence. Both platforms remain fully functional and scientifically valuable. It is, instead, a political choice: a visible cut that signals disengagement from climate monitoring. The House of Representatives has backed the move; the Senate wants to maintain funding. If the House line prevails, the shutdown could be executed within weeks of the budget passing.

For Europe, this is the pivotal moment. What Washington discards for symbolic savings could be preserved at trivial cost, even transformed into a strategic advantage.

### **The Cost of Doing Nothing**

If Europe stands aside, the consequences will be immediate. A decade-long, calibration-consistent dataset will be broken, and that break cannot be repaired later. Treaty verification under the Paris Agreement will lose credibility. Without continuous measurement, it becomes far easier for governments to manipulate reporting or delay action.

The impact would ripple into markets. Carbon pricing schemes and offset verification rely on independent atmospheric checks. Without OCO data, disputes multiply, trust weakens, and the value of carbon markets erodes. Agriculture would feel it too. Crop forecasting models integrate OCO’s photosynthesis data to predict yields. Strip that out and accuracy drops, exposing insurers, commodity traders, and farmers to greater risk.

The satellites cost little to run. But the costs of losing them, in credibility, in commercial disruption, in lost scientific continuity, are orders of magnitude higher. Doing nothing is not just passive, it is actively expensive.

### **Europe’s Gap to Fill**

Europe has built one of the strongest civilian Earth Observation fleets in the world, yet it does not currently have a public system to match OCO’s precision and coverage. Sentinel-5P’s TROPOMI can measure CO₂, but at a much coarser scale. Commercial players like GHGSat can deliver pinpoint methane and CO₂ detection at facility level, but they do not provide the global, open-access record OCO delivers.

The gap will close eventually. France’s MicroCarb launched this year, but as a single satellite its coverage will be limited. ESA’s flagship CO₂M constellation promises world-class capability, but first launches are not expected until 2026/2027 and validation will take time. In practice, that leaves Europe with at least a two- to three-year window without sovereign access to an OCO-class dataset.

Filling that gap is a strategic necessity. The cheapest, fastest way to do it is to take over operations of OCO-2 and OCO-3. These satellites are not Europe’s yet, but they could be, and for a price that is almost laughably small compared to the value they deliver.

### **A Deal on the Table**

Europe does not need to reinvent the wheel. OCO-2 and OCO-3 are already in orbit, fully functional, and producing unmatched carbon data. What they lack is a backer. The annual operations bill sits in the low tens of millions of dollars, modest by space standards, and insignificant compared to the sums already committed to Copernicus.

This is where a deal becomes possible. Washington wants to cut the line item. Europe needs to fill a gap. If ESA or the European Commission steps in, the satellites keep flying, and both sides can declare success. For the US, the politics are straightforward. The budget cut is achieved, and the story becomes one of allies “paying their share.” For Europe, the payoff is continuity of the gold-standard CO₂ dataset, leverage in climate diplomacy, and a stronger hand as MicroCarb and CO₂M come online.

Structurally, the options are simple. Europe could assume the full cost through ESA. A cost-share arrangement is equally feasible, with both sides contributing while Europe secures guaranteed access and a role in setting priorities. Hybrid models could involve philanthropic or commercial co-funding. However it is structured, the mechanism is clear. A small operational outlay preserves a globally critical dataset and allows both Washington and Brussels to claim a win.

### **The Best Bargain in Space**

What makes this opportunity remarkable is the value-for-money. Running OCO-2 and OCO-3 for another three to five years would cost Europe less than one percent of what it is already spending on new satellites. For a fraction of a single Copernicus mission, Europe could buy immediate access to the sharpest CO₂ dataset ever collected.

I ran the numbers, conservatively. OCO-2 cost about $465M to build, launch, and for ground systems, with an addition $10M in operating costs per year. Over ten years this is at least $550M. For OCO-3, it likely cost half that at $250M as it is mounted on the ISS. This means, over a ten year timeframe, the total cost to NASA has been about $700M, or $70M a year. As the system is set to be scrapped, if Europe instead stepped in and provided $15M per year to operate both, that would represent a 79% discount compared to building one ourselves.

The return is outsized. These satellites bridge the two- to three-year gap before MicroCarb and CO₂M are operational, ensuring Europe avoids a break in continuity that would undermine treaty verification and commercial applications alike. They also provide the calibration reference that will make Europe’s own future missions more credible from day one.

No other move in space policy offers such a high ratio of strategic gain to financial cost. For policymakers in Brussels or London, this is the definition of a bargain. Minimal spend, maximum leverage, and an instant upgrade to Europe’s role as the custodian of global carbon data.

### **We’ve Done This Before**

This kind of arrangement is not new. Space agencies have a long history of extending the life of valuable missions through shared funding and operations. Hubble stayed productive for decades thanks to joint NASA–ESA servicing. NOAA and EUMETSAT run weather satellites under a burden-sharing agreement, each partner covering part of the constellation while sharing the data. ESA scientists already rely on ICESat-2, a US satellite, for polar monitoring under international cooperation agreements.

The lesson is simple. When a capability is too valuable to lose, allies step in. OCO-2 and OCO-3 are no different. The instruments are working, the data is irreplaceable, and the cost of preserving them is trivial compared to building a new system. Europe stepping in would not be a radical departure. It would be a continuation of a proven model, pooling resources to protect shared interests in space.

### **Europe’s Leadership Moment**

Stepping in to save OCO-2 and OCO-3 is more than an act of pragmatism. It is a chance to set the tone for global climate leadership. Europe has already positioned itself as the centre of gravity for environmental monitoring through Copernicus and the European Green Deal. Taking over the world’s most precise CO₂ dataset would reinforce that role, sending a clear signal that when others retreat, Europe advances.

The payoff would extend beyond science. Climate diplomacy is a contest of credibility, and the side that controls the definitive dataset shapes the agenda. With OCO-2 and OCO-3 under European stewardship, Brussels would hold the evidence base that underpins treaty verification and market trust. London, Paris, Berlin, and Brussels would be the arbiters of whether national pledges align with atmospheric reality.

This is not only about filling a gap. It is about seizing the mantle of leadership. What Washington views as expendable, Europe can elevate into a defining capability, turning symbolic US cuts into a European strategic advantage.

### **Bridging to CO₂M**

Europe is not short of ambition. MicroCarb is already in orbit, and the Copernicus CO₂M constellation is moving toward launch later this decade. Together they will give Europe sovereign, world-class carbon monitoring capability. But those systems are still commissioning or in development, and their early years will be defined by calibration and validation.

This is where OCO-2 and OCO-3 add unique value. Their decade of continuous measurements provides the baseline against which new European instruments can be cross-calibrated. If Europe funds them through to CO₂M’s entry into service, the continent secures an unbroken data chain from 2014 onwards, a dataset no one else can match. That continuity would strengthen the credibility of MicroCarb and CO₂M from day one, easing adoption by policymakers, markets, and international climate frameworks.

I have not worked directly on climate datasets, but I have spent years in policy and programme analysis across the space sector. One thing has always stood out. Without consistent data, everything else unravels. I have seen major programmes lose credibility because one dataset ended before the next began. Without overlap, you can never be sure whether two systems are telling the same story, and policymakers quickly lose confidence. That gap opens the door to doubt, delay, and debate, exactly what climate policy cannot afford. It is the same principle you see in economics, when the OECD changes a measure they run the old and new side by side. Without that overlap, you do not know whether the data changed or the measurement did.

### **Europe’s Move to Make**

This is not complicated. Two satellites are working. They are producing the best carbon data in the world. The United States wants to trash them to save pocket change.

Europe can step in, and for the price of a rounding error secure the gold-standard CO₂ dataset, bridge its capability gap, and prove that it can lead when others walk away. No committee, no multi-year procurement cycle, no billion-euro budget needed. Just a small cheque and a political decision.

In every programme I have worked on, one truth has stood out. Break the dataset and you break the trust. Without overlap, Europe’s new missions launch into doubt. With OCO, the handover is seamless and the credibility unquestionable.

This is the best bargain in space. Washington will call it a cut. Europe can call it a win. The only question is whether Brussels and London are ready to take it.

The impact would ripple into markets. Carbon pricing schemes and offset verification rely on independent atmospheric checks. Without OCO data, disputes multiply, trust weakens, and the value of carbon markets erodes. Agriculture would feel it too. Crop forecasting models integrate OCO’s photosynthesis data to predict yields. Strip that out and accuracy drops, exposing insurers, commodity traders, and farmers to greater risk.

The satellites cost little to run. But the costs of losing them, in credibility, in commercial disruption, in lost scientific continuity, are orders of magnitude higher. Doing nothing is not just passive, it is actively expensive.

Europe’s Gap to Fill

Europe has built one of the strongest civilian Earth Observation fleets in the world, yet it does not currently have a public system to match OCO’s precision and coverage. Sentinel-5P’s TROPOMI can measure CO₂, but at a much coarser scale. Commercial players like GHGSat can deliver pinpoint methane and CO₂ detection at facility level, but they do not provide the global, open-access record OCO delivers.

The gap will close eventually. France’s MicroCarb launched this year, but as a single satellite its coverage will be limited. ESA’s flagship CO₂M constellation promises world-class capability, but first launches are not expected until 2026/2027 and validation will take time. In practice, that leaves Europe with at least a two- to three-year window without sovereign access to an OCO-class dataset.

Filling that gap is a strategic necessity. The cheapest, fastest way to do it is to take over operations of OCO-2 and OCO-3. These satellites are not Europe’s yet, but they could be, and for a price that is almost laughably small compared to the value they deliver.

A Deal on the Table

Europe does not need to reinvent the wheel. OCO-2 and OCO-3 are already in orbit, fully functional, and producing unmatched carbon data. What they lack is a backer. The annual operations bill sits in the low tens of millions of dollars, modest by space standards, and insignificant compared to the sums already committed to Copernicus.

This is where a deal becomes possible. Washington wants to cut the line item. Europe needs to fill a gap. If ESA or the European Commission steps in, the satellites keep flying, and both sides can declare success. For the US, the politics are straightforward. The budget cut is achieved, and the story becomes one of allies “paying their share.” For Europe, the payoff is continuity of the gold-standard CO₂ dataset, leverage in climate diplomacy, and a stronger hand as MicroCarb and CO₂M come online.

Structurally, the options are simple. Europe could assume the full cost through ESA. A cost-share arrangement is equally feasible, with both sides contributing while Europe secures guaranteed access and a role in setting priorities. Hybrid models could involve philanthropic or commercial co-funding. However it is structured, the mechanism is clear. A small operational outlay preserves a globally critical dataset and allows both Washington and Brussels to claim a win.

The Best Bargain in Space

What makes this opportunity remarkable is the value-for-money. Running OCO-2 and OCO-3 for another three to five years would cost Europe less than one percent of what it is already spending on new satellites. For a fraction of a single Copernicus mission, Europe could buy immediate access to the sharpest CO₂ dataset ever collected.

I ran the numbers, conservatively. OCO-2 cost about $465M to build, launch, and for ground systems, with an addition $10M in operating costs per year. Over ten years this is at least $550M. For OCO-3, it likely cost half that at $250M as it is mounted on the ISS. This means, over a ten year timeframe, the total cost to NASA has been about $700M, or $70M a year. As the system is set to be scrapped, if Europe instead stepped in and provided $15M per year to operate both, that would represent a 79% discount compared to building one ourselves.

The return is outsized. These satellites bridge the two- to three-year gap before MicroCarb and CO₂M are operational, ensuring Europe avoids a break in continuity that would undermine treaty verification and commercial applications alike. They also provide the calibration reference that will make Europe’s own future missions more credible from day one.

No other move in space policy offers such a high ratio of strategic gain to financial cost. For policymakers in Brussels or London, this is the definition of a bargain. Minimal spend, maximum leverage, and an instant upgrade to Europe’s role as the custodian of global carbon data.

We’ve Done This Before

This kind of arrangement is not new. Space agencies have a long history of extending the life of valuable missions through shared funding and operations. Hubble stayed productive for decades thanks to joint NASA–ESA servicing. NOAA and EUMETSAT run weather satellites under a burden-sharing agreement, each partner covering part of the constellation while sharing the data. ESA scientists already rely on ICESat-2, a US satellite, for polar monitoring under international cooperation agreements.

The lesson is simple. When a capability is too valuable to lose, allies step in. OCO-2 and OCO-3 are no different. The instruments are working, the data is irreplaceable, and the cost of preserving them is trivial compared to building a new system. Europe stepping in would not be a radical departure. It would be a continuation of a proven model, pooling resources to protect shared interests in space.

Europe’s Leadership Moment

Stepping in to save OCO-2 and OCO-3 is more than an act of pragmatism. It is a chance to set the tone for global climate leadership. Europe has already positioned itself as the centre of gravity for environmental monitoring through Copernicus and the European Green Deal. Taking over the world’s most precise CO₂ dataset would reinforce that role, sending a clear signal that when others retreat, Europe advances.

The payoff would extend beyond science. Climate diplomacy is a contest of credibility, and the side that controls the definitive dataset shapes the agenda. With OCO-2 and OCO-3 under European stewardship, Brussels would hold the evidence base that underpins treaty verification and market trust. London, Paris, Berlin, and Brussels would be the arbiters of whether national pledges align with atmospheric reality.

This is not only about filling a gap. It is about seizing the mantle of leadership. What Washington views as expendable, Europe can elevate into a defining capability, turning symbolic US cuts into a European strategic advantage.

Bridging to CO₂M

Europe is not short of ambition. MicroCarb is already in orbit, and the Copernicus CO₂M constellation is moving toward launch later this decade. Together they will give Europe sovereign, world-class carbon monitoring capability. But those systems are still commissioning or in development, and their early years will be defined by calibration and validation.

This is where OCO-2 and OCO-3 add unique value. Their decade of continuous measurements provides the baseline against which new European instruments can be cross-calibrated. If Europe funds them through to CO₂M’s entry into service, the continent secures an unbroken data chain from 2014 onwards, a dataset no one else can match. That continuity would strengthen the credibility of MicroCarb and CO₂M from day one, easing adoption by policymakers, markets, and international climate frameworks.

I have not worked directly on climate datasets, but I have spent years in policy and programme analysis across the space sector. One thing has always stood out. Without consistent data, everything else unravels. I have seen major programmes lose credibility because one dataset ended before the next began. Without overlap, you can never be sure whether two systems are telling the same story, and policymakers quickly lose confidence. That gap opens the door to doubt, delay, and debate, exactly what climate policy cannot afford. It is the same principle you see in economics, when the OECD changes a measure they run the old and new side by side. Without that overlap, you do not know whether the data changed or the measurement did.

Europe’s Move to Make

This is not complicated. Two satellites are working. They are producing the best carbon data in the world. The United States wants to trash them to save pocket change.

Europe can step in, and for the price of a rounding error secure the gold-standard CO₂ dataset, bridge its capability gap, and prove that it can lead when others walk away. No committee, no multi-year procurement cycle, no billion-euro budget needed. Just a small cheque and a political decision.

In every programme I have worked on, one truth has stood out. Break the dataset and you break the trust. Without overlap, Europe’s new missions launch into doubt. With OCO, the handover is seamless and the credibility unquestionable.

This is the best bargain in space. Washington will call it a cut. Europe can call it a win. The only question is whether Brussels and London are ready to take it.
